en/forms/index.title: Forms
en/forms/index.content:
A static website cannot send mail. quartz-forms gives a Quartz website forms all the same:
contact, feedback, sign-up, survey. They are described once in quartz.config.yaml, embedded on
any page, checked in the browser and, if wanted, encrypted with OpenPGP before they leave the page.
They are delivered by a small PHP script on your own web space or by a form service.


                  
                  The forms in this handbook send nothing 
                  
                

Every form here runs with transport: { kind: demo }. It checks and encrypts as on a real
website and then shows below itself what would have arrived. Trying them out is very much
intended.



What it does


                  
                  Describe once, embed anywhere 
                  
                

A form is an entry under options.forms. A page pulls it in with a code block, a placeholder or
a frontmatter key; through the layout it stands on every page. → 3




                  
                  Fifteen field types, widths, conditions, steps 
                  
                

From a line of text to a scale, side by side or stacked, fields that appear only when they are
needed, and long forms in steps. → 2, 4




                  
                  Encrypted before it leaves the page 
                  
                

OpenPGP runs in the visitor’s browser. Neither the server nor a service sees the plain text, only
the mailbox with the matching key. → 6.2




                  
                  The address never reaches the website 
                  
                

The bundled relay knows the recipients’ addresses, the website only a name. Spam protection
without third-party services comes with it. → 5,
6.3


The chapters













































ChapterWhat it covers1 – Getting startedWhat the plugin is for, the first form, what happens at build time2 – FieldsThe field types, required fields and rules, width and arrangement3 – EmbeddingCode block, placeholder, frontmatter and layout4 – FlowConditions, steps and what happens without JavaScript5 – SendingThe transports, the relay and how it gets onto your web space6 – ProtectionAnonymous forms, encryption, spam7 – AppearanceTexts and languages, CSS variables, markup8 – RecipesFinished forms for common cases9 – ReferenceEvery option, every message, the limits
With QuartzControl
QuartzControl edits the forms in the “Forms” tab of
the plugins page: fields by drag and drop, checking keys, generating and uploading the relay. This
handbook describes what that writes into quartz.config.yaml.
Licence
quartz-forms is under the MIT licence. OpenPGP.js, which it ships as a separate
file, is under LGPL-3.0-or-later.

en/index.title: Four plugins for Quartz
en/index.content:
Four plugins for Quartz, each with a handbook of its own. They can be
used on their own and work together; this website is built with all four.


                  
                  Layout Box 
                  
                

A piece of HTML or Markdown anywhere in the layout: a wordmark, a notice, a line with the page’s
status. → To the handbook




                  
                  Multilanguage 
                  
                

The same notes in several languages from one vault, with a switcher, hreflang and a notice
in the visitor’s language. → To the handbook




                  
                  Navigations 
                  
                

Navigations from the folder structure, as many as needed and in ten variants: menu bar,
accordion, sitemap, “Previous” and “Next”. → To the handbook




                  
                  Forms 
                  
                

Forms for a static website, checked in the browser and, if wanted, encrypted with OpenPGP.
→ To the handbook


With QuartzControl
All four can be installed in QuartzControl and set up
without YAML. The app is not required: every handbook also shows the entry in quartz.config.yaml.
Licence
All four plugins are under the MIT licence. The source is on GitHub:
quartz-layout-box,
quartz-multilanguage,
quartz-navigations and
quartz-forms.

en/layout-box/1-getting-started/01-why-t.title: 1.1 – Why this plugin
en/layout-box/1-getting-started/01-why-t.content:
Quartz builds every page from components: explorer, table of contents, breadcrumbs, footer. Each has
a job and fills itself from the content of the site. What does not exist is a component for this —
the line under the site name, the logo, the notice that the site is still being built.
Without this plugin there are two ways to get one, and neither is good:

Write it into the theme. Then the text lives in a .tsx file, changing a comma needs a
compile, and the next Quartz update collides with it.
Write it into every page. Then it sits in the vault 200 times and goes wrong 200 times as soon
as anything changes.

The layout box is the third way: one snippet, maintained in one place, placed at one point in the
layout.
What it does
It takes a piece of HTML or Markdown and puts it where you tell it — left or right sidebar, header,
footer, before or after the page body. The text comes either from a file under
quartz/static/snippets/ or straight from the configuration.
All of it happens at build time. What reaches the browser is finished HTML; the plugin ships no
JavaScript, and a box costs the page nothing in load time.
What it does not do
It is not a building block for content. What belongs on one page belongs in that page. The box
is for what is the same across many pages.
It does not render Obsidian syntax. A Markdown snippet does not go through Quartz’ content
pipeline — wikilinks in double square brackets and callouts stay as written. Why that is, and what
works instead, is under 2.3 – Markdown snippets.
And it filters nothing. A snippet is inserted as it stands; whoever embeds foreign HTML embeds
foreign HTML. See 9.3 – Limits.
When it is worth it


                  
                  The rule of thumb 
                  
                

As soon as the same piece of markup should appear on more than one page and is not part of the
text, it belongs in a layout box.


Seven examples, all of them visible on this site, are in chapter 8. The
shortest is the line in the footer carrying the site name; the most elaborate is the word mark at
the top left, which switches between the light and dark colour scheme without a line of JavaScript
being involved.

en/layout-box/1-getting-started/02-your-.title: 1.2 – Your first box
en/layout-box/1-getting-started/02-your-.content:
Four steps, and the box is there.
1. Install the plugin
npx quartz plugin add github:boxi-os/quartz-layout-box
The command fetches the plugin and adds it to quartz.config.yaml. In
QuartzControl the same happens through the marketplace.
2. Create a snippet
The file goes into quartz/static/snippets/ — that folder belongs to the site, not to the content.
It is created if it is missing:
<!-- quartz/static/snippets/snippet.html -->
<p>Notes from a small town.</p>
3. Add the entry
plugins:
  - source: github:boxi-os/quartz-layout-box
    enabled: true
    options:
      file: snippet.html
    layout:
      position: left
      priority: 15
position says where, priority in what order within that place — smaller means further up. Both
are explained in chapter 3.


                  
                  It works without options too
                  
                

Then the defaults apply: the file snippet.html in the folder quartz/static/snippets.


4. Look at it
npx quartz build --serve
The box sits in the left column. Change the snippet file now and a reload is enough — no restart
of the server. Why that works without a watcher is under
1.3 – What happens at build time.
When nothing appears

























What you seeWhat causes itA dashed box with a path in itThe file is missing at exactly that place. The box only appears in serve mode; in a normal build the box stays empty and the console says so once.Nothing at all, no messageThe snippet is empty. A box without content outputs nothing — not even an empty div.Nothing, but a warning during the buildThe path leads out of dir. The plugin refuses that; see 2.2 – Where the file comes from.The box is there, in the wrong placeposition or priority — 3.2 – The order.

en/layout-box/1-getting-started/03-what-.title: 1.3 – What happens at build time
en/layout-box/1-getting-started/03-what-.content:
Quartz loads the plugin as a pure component. Every entry in quartz.config.yaml that has a layout
block becomes its own instance with its own options. An entry without a layout block does not
disappear: Quartz places any component that names no position at its manifest’s default — for this
plugin left, with priority: 15. Building each page then runs the same sequence:

Check the frontmatter — is the box hidden on this page? Was a different snippet chosen? Does
the page have a language that byLang knows something about?
Determine the source — html from the configuration wins, otherwise the file from dir and
file.
Read the file — the path has to lie inside dir. Reading is cached: reloaded only when the
modification time has changed.
Render Markdown — if the file ends in .md, it becomes HTML. That result is cached too.
Replace placeholders — page and site values are inserted and escaped along the way.
Emit — a div with the class layout-box, optionally with a heading or as a collapsible
details.

Why reloading works without a restart
Step 3 asks for the file’s modification time on every render. If it is the same as last time,
the content comes from the cache; if it is newer, the file is read.
So a change to the snippet takes effect immediately under --serve, and it needs no file watcher
that somebody would have to set up and tear down. In a normal build the same approach costs exactly
one filesystem stat per page — measurable, but weightless next to the rest of a build.


                  
                  What follows from that 
                  
                

The cache hangs on the modification time, not on the content. Writing a file back with the same
timestamp — restoring from an archive, say — shows the old version until the time changes.


A pure component, not a transformer
The plugin does not reach into the content pipeline. It sees no note, changes no text and never
walks the vault. It is asked only when Quartz assembles the layout of a page.
That is why a Markdown snippet resolves no wikilinks: the place where Quartz does that sort of thing
is long behind the box.

en/layout-box/1-getting-started/index.title: 1 – Getting started
en/layout-box/1-getting-started/index.content:
Three pages, after which a box stands and you know why.





















PageContent1.1 – Why this pluginWhat Quartz does on its own, and where it stops1.2 – Your first boxInstall, create a snippet, add the entry, look at it1.3 – What happens at build timeThe six steps per page — and why reloading works without a restart

en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/01-file-or-c.title: 2.1 – File or configuration
en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/01-file-or-c.content:
A box’s content comes from a file or straight from the configuration:
options:
  file: snippet.html   # -> snippets/snippet.html
options:
  html: "<p>Notes from a small town.</p>"


                  
                   html always wins
                  
                

With both present, file is not even read. That does not deserve an error message, but it is a
common confusion: someone creates a file, it does not appear, and an html from an earlier
attempt is still sitting in the entry.


When to use which






























File (file)Configuration (html)Sizemore than two or three linesone-linersEditingin an editor, with syntax highlightingin the YAML file, with its escaping rulesIn serve modea change takes effect on reloada change needs a restartIn a template packagetravels through the Static files parttravels inside the entry itself
The last point surprises people most often — and it is why the Example template for QuartzControl
fills six of its seven boxes with html: a template package without the Static files part does
not carry snippet files, and a file: box then pointed at nothing in the target project.
YAML and markup get along moderately
Multi-line HTML in YAML needs a block scalar. | keeps the line breaks, >- folds them into spaces
and swallows the last one:
options:
  html: |
    <p>First line.</p>
    <p>Second line.</p>
As soon as quotation marks, colons and hash signs appear in the markup — which is to say almost
always — a file is the calmer way.

en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/02-where-the.title: 2.2 – Where the file comes from
en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/02-where-the.content:
file is a name inside dir. The default for dir is quartz/static/snippets, counted from
the root of the site:
options:
  dir: quartz/static/snippets   # default
  file: snippet.html            # -> darin
Subfolders are allowed: file: header/mark.html reads
quartz/static/snippets/header/mark.html.
The line
A path leading out of dir is refused — the box outputs nothing and the build warns once:
options:
  file: ../../../etc/passwd   # refused
What is checked is not the string but the resolved path. A .. in the middle of the name helps as
little as a link pointing out of the folder.


                  
                  Why a line at all 
                  
                

The configuration of a Quartz site gets passed around — as a template package, as a repository, as
an example in a forum. A file allowed to read any path on the machine would turn a shared entry
into a tool for reading other people’s files. The line costs nothing and rules that out.


Why quartz/static/
The folder belongs to the site, not to the content. That is deliberate: a snippet is design, and
design has no business in the vault — otherwise it shows up in the explorer, in the search and in
the graph.
Everything under quartz/static/ is shipped by Quartz anyway. Which also means: the snippet files
themselves are reachable through the site’s address. For markup that appears on every page anyway
that is of no consequence — but it is not a place for anything meant to stay private.

en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/03-markdown-.title: 2.3 – Markdown snippets
en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/03-markdown-.content:
If file ends in .md, the file is turned into HTML at build time. What is rendered is
GitHub-Flavored Markdown, embedded HTML is allowed, and placeholders work as they do elsewhere:
## {{siteTitle}}
 
Notes from a _small_ town.
 
- <a href="{{root}}/about">About this site</a>
- <a href="{{root}}/contact">Contact</a>
The box at the bottom left of this site is made exactly that way — with Markdown links, ever since
the plugin learned to recognise the encoded form. Why that did not work for a while, and when an HTML
anchor is still the safer way, is right below.
What does not work there
A Markdown snippet does not go through Quartz’ content pipeline. What stays as written:

































WrittenWhat becomes of it[[wikilink]]stays as text> [!note]becomes an ordinary quote, not a callout![[image.png]]stays as text[text](target)becomes a link — ordinary Markdown works[text]({{root}}/target)becomes a link with the value filled in — see below**bold**, lists, tables, headingsall work
The reason is in 1.3: the plugin is a pure
component. It is asked when Quartz builds the layout — and by then the content has long been
processed.
A placeholder in a link target — the story behind it
That the line above works has not been true for long, and the reason is worth knowing.
Markdown is rendered to HTML first, placeholders are replaced afterwards
(1.3). While rendering, the Markdown renderer
turns a link target into an address and escapes the curly braces to %7B%7B and %7D%7D. The
replacement then looked for {{root}} and found nothing; the HTML literally said
%7B%7Broot%7D%7D.
Inside the href of an HTML element that never happened — there the address stays as it is until
the replacement reaches it. Two spellings that look equivalent in the source behaved differently.


                  
                  Fixed, but not retroactively 
                  
                

The plugin now recognises the encoded form and treats both spellings alike. Anyone on an older
version writes links in a snippet as HTML anchors:
<a href="{{root}}/about">About this site</a>. That works in every version.




                  
                  Only found on publishing 
                  
                

As long as a site sits at the root, a broken path barely shows. Under a subpath — the normal case
on GitHub Pages — every one of those links led nowhere. That is exactly how it came out: on the
first deploy of these four sites, 14 dead links at once.




                  
                  Links in a snippet want {{root}}
                  
                

A snippet appears on every page, including those two levels down. A link to /about misses the
server root as soon as the site lives under a subpath. {{root}}/about works the way out from
every page; see 4.2 – root and addresses.


HTML or Markdown?
Markdown pays off as soon as the snippet holds prose, a list or links — it is shorter and reads
better while editing. HTML pays off as soon as structure is involved that Markdown does not know: an
<svg>, an image with a light and a dark variant, an element with a class of its own.

en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/index.title: 2 – The snippet
en/layout-box/2-the-snippet/index.content:
A box has exactly one source. Which it can be, and when which one is better.





















PageContent2.1 – File or configurationfile against html, and which one wins2.2 – Where the file comes fromThe dir folder and the line it draws2.3 – Markdown snippetsWhen the file ends in .md — and what does not work there

en/layout-box/3-placement/01-the-six-pla.title: 3.1 – The six places
en/layout-box/3-placement/01-the-six-pla.content:
layout:
  position: left
Six values are possible:








































positionWhere that isWhat it is good forheaderthe bar at the very top, beside title and searchword mark, page name, a short badgeleftleft column, under the explorersite description, a note, navigation helprightright column, by the table of contentsnotes on the chapter, a contact boxbeforeBodybetween breadcrumbs and titlebanners concerning the whole page: version, warning, draft statusafterBodyunder the text, above the backlinksa call to action, a read-on box, a donation noticefooterthe footer at the very bottomcolophon, imprint line, a line stating where things stand
What the place decides about the form
The same component looks right in a different way at each place. A box in the header is a word mark
— short, one line, no frame. The same box after the body may have area, a bar, a heading. In the
footer it is a small, centred line.
The plugin brings nothing for that: it sets layout-box as a class and whatever is in className.
What a place looks like is decided by the site’s CSS — 5.2 – Styling shows
it on the four boxes of this site.


                  
                   beforeBody and afterBody have the full text width
                  
                

The two columns are narrow; what sits there has to work in about 300 pixels. Before and after the
body a box has the whole width of the text column — the right place for anything that needs lines.


Groups
Quartz can combine several components at the same place into a group, which then sits side by side
instead of stacked:
layout:
  position: header
  group: brand
That is a Quartz feature, not one of the plugin’s. The word mark and the chapter name at the top of
this page sit side by side that way — two boxes in one group.

en/layout-box/3-placement/02-the-order.title: 3.2 – The order
en/layout-box/3-placement/02-the-order.content:
Several components sit at one place. priority says in what order — smaller means further up:
layout:
  position: left
  priority: 40
The left column of this site:

















priorityComponent30explorer40the note box (“About this handbook”)
Which is why it sits under the explorer. With priority: 20 it would sit above.
The numbers do not come from the plugin
Every component carries a default, and the plugin’s is 15. Whether that means top or bottom
depends on what else is at that place — a number on its own says nothing. Whoever wants to move a
box looks at its neighbours’ numbers, not at its own.


                  
                  Leave gaps 
                  
                

10, 20, 30 rather than 1, 2, 3. Then something can be slipped in later without three other entries
needing new numbers.


order is something else
Besides layout.priority there is order at the level of the entry:
- source: github:boxi-os/quartz-layout-box
  order: 500          # load order of the plugins
  layout:
    priority: 40      # order on the page
order decides when Quartz loads the plugin — for a pure component with no bearing on the
rendering. priority decides where the box sits. The two get confused readily, because both
sound like order.

en/layout-box/3-placement/03-the-same-bo.title: 3.3 – The same box twice
en/layout-box/3-placement/03-the-same-bo.content:
The plugin may appear in the configuration more than once. Every entry becomes its own instance with
its own options and its own place.
plugins:
  - source: github:boxi-os/quartz-layout-box
    options:
      file: snippet.html
      frontmatterKey: layoutBoxNote
    layout:
      position: left
      display: desktop-only
 
  - source: github:boxi-os/quartz-layout-box
    options:
      file: snippet-mobile.html
      className: layout-box-mobile
      frontmatterKey: layoutBoxMobile
    layout:
      position: afterBody
      display: mobile-only
display





















ValueEffectalleverywhere (default)desktop-onlyfrom tablet width upwardsmobile-onlyonly below it
The switching width belongs to the site, not to the plugin. It is the same one that makes the
explorer and the table of contents disappear.


                  
                   display hides, it does not rebuild
                  
                

Both boxes are in the HTML of every page; CSS shows only one. For a few lines of markup that does
not matter, for an inline SVG in two variants every page grows by both.


Every instance wants its own frontmatterKey
Without their own keys, all instances listen to the same field — layoutBox: false would then hide
all of them. As soon as there is more than one, each gets its own:
options:
  frontmatterKey: layoutBoxNote     # instead of the default layoutBox
The four boxes of this site are called layoutBoxMark, layoutBoxPageName, layoutBoxNote — and
the fourth has none at all, because no page should ever steer it. Why that is a deliberate decision
is in 8.2 – The invisible box.
className per instance too
All boxes carry layout-box. To tell them apart in CSS, each gets an extra class of its own —
layout-box-mark, layout-box-note. Without those you would have to select by position in the
layout, which breaks the first time anything is reordered.

en/layout-box/3-placement/index.title: 3 – Placement
en/layout-box/3-placement/index.content:
The layout block decides the place. It belongs to Quartz, not to the plugin — the same rules apply
to every component.





















PageContent3.1 – The six placesWhere a box can go, and what each place is good for3.2 – The orderpriority, and why the box ends up under the explorer3.3 – The same box twicedisplay for smartphone and desktop, several instances

en/layout-box/4-placeholders/01-every-pl.title: 4.1 – Every placeholder
en/layout-box/4-placeholders/01-every-pl.content:
Placeholders sit in double curly braces and are replaced anew on every page. Spaces inside the
braces are allowed: {{ title }} is the same as {{title}}.









































PlaceholderValue{{title}}the page’s title from the frontmatter{{slug}}the page’s path, such as 3-placement/02-the-order{{root}}relative way to the site root — . on the start page, ../.. two levels down{{siteTitle}}configuration.pageTitle from the Quartz configuration{{baseUrl}}configuration.baseUrl, may be empty{{locale}}the page’s language: frontmatter field lang, else configuration.locale — en-US, say{{lang}}only the front part of it: en{{frontmatter.field}}any frontmatter field of the page
Values are escaped
An & in a page title becomes &amp;, angle brackets are made harmless. A placeholder therefore
cannot smuggle in markup — not even when somebody writes <script> into a title.
Unknown names stay put
{{doesnotexist}} does not become an empty spot; it stays visible in the text. That is deliberate: a
typo shows itself on first sight instead of quietly leaving a hole.
Anyone who needs curly braces as text switches the replacement off for that box:
options:
  placeholders: false
Frontmatter fields
{{frontmatter.<field>}} reads any field of the page. The chapter name in this site’s header is
exactly that:
options:
  html: '<span data-section="{{frontmatter.section}}"></span>'

























What the field holdsWhat gets insertedtext or a numberthe valuea listjoined with commas: a, b, can objectnothing — the placeholder staysthe field is missingnothing — the placeholder stays


                  
                  Placeholders work in the title too 
                  
                

title: "About {{siteTitle}}" works. The plugin just does not escape there itself — the heading is
a text node, which Preact escapes anyway.

en/layout-box/4-placeholders/02-root-and.title: 4.2 – root and addresses
en/layout-box/4-placeholders/02-root-and.content:
A snippet appears on every page — on the start page and on one three levels down. A link inside it
has to be right from everywhere. That is what {{root}} is for.
<a href="{{root}}/about">About this site</a>

























From which pageWhat it becomesstart page./about3-placement/index../about3-placement/02-the-order../abouta/b/c../../about
What is counted is the slug’s segments minus one. 3-placement/index and
3-placement/02-the-order both have two segments and therefore sit equally deep — that one is a
folder page and the other is not makes no difference.
Why not simply /about
A leading slash points at the server root. As long as the site sits there, that works fine. As
soon as it sits under a subpath, it points straight past it:




















Address of the site/about lands at{{root}}/about lands atexample.orgexample.org/about ✓the same ✓boxi-os.github.io/quartz-pluginsboxi-os.github.io/about ✗…/quartz-plugins/about ✓
The second case is the normal one on GitHub Pages — and the reason this site writes its own links
that way.


                  
                  The mistake only shows after publishing 
                  
                

Locally the preview runs on localhost without a subpath, where the slash works. It breaks
exactly where nobody is watching any more.


Images likewise
<img class="img-light" src="{{root}}/static/logo-light.png" alt="" />
<img class="img-dark" src="{{root}}/static/logo-dark.png" alt="" />
The two classes are part of the plugin: img-light appears in the light colour scheme, img-dark
in the dark one. The plugin sets display for both itself — so write no display rule for them
in your own CSS. It would beat the plugin’s, and both images would stand there at once. At length in
5.2 – Styling.
Absolute addresses stay absolute
{{baseUrl}} returns the configured address of the site — for cases where a link has to be absolute
rather than relative: an og:url, a feed, a line meant to be copied.

en/layout-box/4-placeholders/index.title: 4 – Placeholders
en/layout-box/4-placeholders/index.content:
A snippet appears the same on every page — except where a placeholder stands.

















PageContent4.1 – Every placeholderThe list, with the value per page4.2 – root and addressesWhy /about breaks and {{root}}/about does not

en/layout-box/5-form/01-title-and-collap.title: 5.1 – Title and collapsing
en/layout-box/5-form/01-title-and-collap.content:
Heading
options:
  title: About this handbook
That becomes an h3 with the class layout-box-title — the same level the explorer and the table
of contents use for their headings, so that the page’s outline stays sound.
Placeholders work here too: title: "About {{siteTitle}}".
Collapsing
options:
  title: About this handbook
  collapsible: true
  collapsed: false
collapsible turns the box into a details element whose clickable line is the title. collapsed
decides whether it starts closed. The box at the bottom left of this site is built exactly that way —
only with collapsed: true, so it starts closed.


                  
                   collapsible without title does not work
                  
                

A details with no line to click could not be opened. The plugin says so at build time —
“collapsible requires a title; rendering non-collapsible” — and renders the box normally.
The message only appears when collapsible comes from the configuration, from the base options or
from byLang. From a page’s frontmatter it stays away: the box is not collapsible there
either, but without a word.


No JavaScript, with the consequences
Opening and closing is the built-in behaviour of details. No script, no load time, and it works
with JavaScript switched off.
The price: the state does not survive a page change. Open the box, click on, and the next page
shows it the way collapsed says. Anything else would need a script and browser storage — and then
it would no longer be a plugin that ships nothing.


                  
                  Start closed when the box is long 
                  
                

In a narrow column an open box pushes everything below it out of sight. collapsed: true is
usually the friendlier choice there — the title says what is inside, after all.

en/layout-box/5-form/02-styling.title: 5.2 – Styling

en/layout-box/5-form/index.title: 5 – Form
en/layout-box/5-form/index.content:
What the plugin offers in the way of form, and where styling begins.

















PageContent5.1 – Title and collapsingtitle, collapsible, collapsed — without JavaScript5.2 – StylingThe markup produced, the classes, the rules that ship with it

en/layout-box/6-per-page/01-hiding-and-s.title: 6.1 – Hiding and swapping
en/layout-box/6-per-page/01-hiding-and-s.content:
Every instance listens to one frontmatter field. What it is called is set by frontmatterKey;
without one it is layoutBox.
The four forms
Hide it:
---
layoutBox: false
---
A different snippet:
---
layoutBox: imprint.html
---
The name is relative to dir, exactly as in the configuration.
Several things at once:
---
layoutBox:
  file: imprint.html
  title: About this page
  collapsed: true
---
Different markup for this page only:
---
layoutBox:
  html: "<p>This page is a draft.</p>"
---
Written as an object, hidden, file, html, title, collapsible and collapsed are allowed.
dir and frontmatterKey are not — one is an installation path, the other the name the page is
speaking under right now.
The order of precedence
From strong to weak:

the page’s frontmatter
byLang for the page’s language (chapter 7)
the base options from the configuration

Each level overrides only what it names itself. A frontmatter with title: leaves file: from the
configuration untouched.


                  
                   html against file does not follow the precedence
                  
                

The source is not decided per level but once for all of them: if there is an html anywhere —
in the frontmatter, under byLang or in the base options — it is taken, and file is never looked
at. So a layoutBox: imprint.html in the frontmatter does nothing when the configuration uses
html:, and a byLang.en.file does nothing when the base options have html:. Without a message.
Measured; and it is exactly what the empty-file trick in
6.2 rests on.


An example that comes up often
A site has a donation box after the body — on the imprint page it feels wrong:
---
title: Imprint
layoutBoxDonate: false
---

en/layout-box/6-per-page/02-what-does-no.title: 6.2 – What does not work
en/layout-box/6-per-page/02-what-does-no.content:
The frontmatter can hide a box, swap its snippet and change its title. What it cannot do
is switch on a box that would not otherwise exist.
The reason is in the construction. An instance comes from an entry in the configuration and runs on
every page; the frontmatter is read once it is already there. There is no way to create an instance
from inside a page that the configuration does not know about.
The way round: empty by default
It is wanted as soon as a box should appear on one page only — a download box on the start page,
say. Showing it everywhere and hiding it again on 200 pages is no solution.
Inverting it is one: the box gets an empty snippet as its default, and the one page swaps it for
the content.
# in the configuration
options:
  file: empty.html                # a file of 0 bytes
  frontmatterKey: layoutBoxDownload
---
# on the start page only
layoutBoxDownload: download.html
---
This works because a box without content outputs nothing at all — no empty div, no spacing, no
element in the HTML. On the other 199 pages the instance is there and stays silent.


                  
                  Two cases where a wrapper does stay behind 
                  
                

Quartz wraps a component with display: desktop-only or mobile-only in a div of its own, and
every member of a group in a div of the flex row. Those wrappers are created before the box is
asked, and therefore stay even when it returns nothing — an empty div, measured. Without
display and without group the sentence above holds exactly.




                  
                  Why an empty file and not an empty html
                  
                

html: "" in the configuration would be shorter and does not work: html takes precedence over
file even when empty — the swap through file in the frontmatter would never get its turn. The
empty file keeps the way through file open.


That is exactly how the download box sits on the start page of
QuartzControl, while the embedded copy of the same
handbook knows nothing about it.
What else does not work

A box per folder. There is no rule saying “applies to everything under notes/”. What helps:
a field in the frontmatter of the pages concerned, or a template in the vault that carries it.
Conditions. No expressions, no comparisons. The frontmatter names values, not rules.
Order per page. priority applies to the site.

en/layout-box/6-per-page/index.title: 6 – Per page
en/layout-box/6-per-page/index.content:
The configuration applies to every page. What a single one wants differently, it says in its
frontmatter.

















PageContent6.1 – Hiding and swappingThe four forms of the frontmatter field6.2 – What does not workWhy a page cannot switch on a box — and what helps instead

en/layout-box/7-two-languages/01-bylang.title: 7.1 – byLang
en/layout-box/7-two-languages/01-bylang.content:
options:
  file: sidebar-note.md
  title: Über dieses Handbuch
  collapsible: true
  byLang:
    en:
      file: sidebar-note.en.md
      title: About this handbook
That is the entry the box at the bottom left of this site comes from — German as the base, English
under byLang.
Where the language comes from
What is read is the page’s frontmatter field lang — the same field Quartz builds its
<html lang> from. If the page has none, configuration.locale applies.
The plugin needs no further plugin for this. Whether lang is written by hand or set by a
multilingual plugin makes no difference to it.
How the keys are matched
Case does not matter. The lookup happens in two passes:

exact — en-US finds the entry en-US
by the front part — en-US also finds the entry en

If nothing matches, the base options apply. Without a warning, because that is the normal case: a
bilingual site names only the second language under byLang, and every page of the first quietly
falls through to the base.
What can differ per language
Everything except two things: dir and frontmatterKey.
One is an installation path, the other the name a page uses to address the box — neither is a
question of language. If the key changed per language, a translated page would have to write a
different field than its original.


                  
                  Forbidden here means: not intended 
                  
                

The TypeScript type does not allow those two under byLang — but a quartz.config.yaml is not
type-checked. A byLang.en.dir therefore does take effect, measured. For frontmatterKey the
sentence holds in practice as well: the key is read before byLang applies at all.


The order of precedence, in full

the page’s frontmatter
byLang for the page’s language
the base options

Each level overrides only what it names. So the entry above keeps collapsible: true from the base
options under en — only what differs is written there.
With one exception: html and file do not sit side by side, they sit against each other. An html
on a weaker level beats any file on a stronger one — see the box in
6.1.

en/layout-box/7-two-languages/02-working.title: 7.2 – Working together
en/layout-box/7-two-languages/02-working.content:
The layout box needs one frontmatter field called lang. Who writes it is none of its concern.
Without a further plugin
A site with a handful of translated pages manages without one:
---
title: Über uns
lang: de
---
From there byLang.de applies. That is enough for a bilingual start page or an imprint in two
versions.
With quartz-multilanguage
As soon as whole language trees are involved, maintaining the field by hand becomes tedious. Then
quartz-multilanguage sets it itself — from the
folder name (en/…), from a file suffix (note.en.md) or from the frontmatter. It also brings the
language switcher this site carries at the top right.
For the layout box nothing changes: it still reads only lang.
Order matters in one place
order decides when Quartz loads a plugin. The layout box is a pure component and reads the
frontmatter only when the page is built — by which time every transformer has long written whatever
it had to write.


                  
                  So there is no order to observe here 
                  
                

Anyone using both plugins has nothing to set in order. The value recommended for
quartz-multilanguage (order: 65, after crawl-links) concerns its own work on the content, not
its interplay with this box.


Two files instead of two entries
A common detour is to create one instance per language and keep them apart with display or
frontmatter. That works, but costs two entries, two frontmatterKeys and double the maintenance.
byLang exists for this.

en/layout-box/7-two-languages/index.title: 7 – Two languages
en/layout-box/7-two-languages/index.content:
This site exists in German and English, and the box at the bottom left reads correctly in both. How
that works is here.

















PageContent7.1 – byLangOptions per language, and how the language is found7.2 – Working togetherWhat quartz-multilanguage adds — and what is not needed

en/layout-box/8-recipes/01-the-four-boxe.title: 8.1 – The four boxes of this site
en/layout-box/8-recipes/01-the-four-boxe.content:
KeyPlaceSourceWhat is on showlayoutBoxMarkheader, priority: 10htmltwo images for light/dark, {{root}}, {{siteTitle}}layoutBoxPageNameheader, priority: 30html{{frontmatter.section}} in an attributelayoutBoxNoteleft, priority: 40file with .mdMarkdown, byLang, collapsible—footer, priority: 20html{{slug}} inside a CSS selector
The word mark
options:
  html: <a class="site-mark" href="{{root}}/"><img
    class="img-light" src="{{root}}/static/icon.png" width="26"
    height="26" alt=""><img class="img-dark"
    src="{{root}}/static/icon-dark.png" width="26" height="26"
    alt=""><span class="site-mark-text">{{siteTitle}}</span></a>
  className: layout-box-mark
  placeholders: true
  frontmatterKey: layoutBoxMark

Two images, one per colour scheme. img-light and img-dark are classes of the plugin; it
shows the matching one and needs no JavaScript for it (5.2).
They are the images Quartz has anyway: icon.png is the favicon, icon-dark.png the variant
for dark mode. Replacing the image replaces favicon and mark in one go — in
QuartzControl under Configuration → Project image.
{{siteTitle}} puts the site title from the configuration next to it, {{root}} makes the
link and the image addresses right, subpath or not
(4.2).
alt="", because the title stands beside it as text; a screen reader would read the name twice
otherwise.

The chapter name
options:
  html: '<span data-section="{{frontmatter.section}}"></span>'
  className: layout-box-page-name
The span stays empty. The value becomes visible only through CSS:
.layout-box-page-name span::before {
  content: "· " attr(data-section);
}
Why the detour? Because the separator and the spacing then belong to the CSS, where they belong —
and because a page without a section shows nothing rather than a lonely dot.
The note box
The only one with file:, and the only one with byLang. It shows three things at once: a Markdown
snippet, two languages and the collapsing.
options:
  file: sidebar-note.md
  title: Über dieses Handbuch
  collapsible: true
  frontmatterKey: layoutBoxNote
  byLang:
    en:
      file: sidebar-note.en.md
      title: About this handbook
layout:
  position: left
  priority: 40
  display: desktop-only
desktop-only, because the left column disappears on a smartphone anyway.
The fourth box has a page of its own: 8.2.

en/layout-box/8-recipes/02-the-invisible.title: 8.2 – The invisible box
en/layout-box/8-recipes/02-the-invisible.content:
The fourth box of this site is not a box in the usual sense. It sits in the footer, is not visible
itself, and outputs only this:
options:
  html: <style>.explorer .folder-container[data-folderpath="{{slug}}"]{…}</style>
  className: layout-box-current-folder
layout:
  position: footer
  priority: 20
It highlights, in the explorer, the folder the currently open page lives in.
Why there is no other way
The explorer writes each folder’s path into the HTML as an attribute. Which of them is the
current one is known only to the page itself — and that is exactly the value {{slug}} supplies.
CSS alone cannot do it: a stylesheet is the same for every page and knows nothing about the current
one. A script could, but that would be JavaScript for a background colour.
Here the placeholder sits inside a selector, not in a text node. That is the unusual part, and it
works because the replacement assumes nothing about the meaning of its surroundings.
Why in the footer
Because it makes no difference where a <style> sits — and the footer is the place where an
invisible box is in nobody’s way. In a sidebar it would, in the awkward case, leave a gap behind.


                  
                  When this would be the wrong way 
                  
                

For styling that is the same on all pages, CSS belongs in custom.scss. The detour through a
box only pays off when a value of the current page has to end up in the rule. Anyone who starts
shipping whole stylesheets this way has moved their CSS into the configuration — hard to read, hard
to change, and freshly in the HTML of every page.


No frontmatterKey
It has none, deliberately: there is no case in which a single page would want to switch the folder
highlight off. A key nobody needs is just another line for somebody to understand later.

en/layout-box/8-recipes/03-more-recipes.title: 8.3 – More recipes
en/layout-box/8-recipes/03-more-recipes.content:
Three recipes not on show on this site — they come from the Example template for QuartzControl, which
this design is derived from.
The call to action after the body
options:
  html: >-
    <p><strong>Read on</strong><br />This page belongs to
    <a href="{{root}}/">{{siteTitle}}</a>.</p>
  className: layout-box-cta
  frontmatterKey: layoutBoxCta
layout:
  position: afterBody
  priority: 20
afterBody, because it needs the full text width. Through layoutBoxCta: false a single page takes
it out again — the imprint, for instance.
The notice only on the smartphone
options:
  html: "<p>The menu is behind the icon at the top left.</p>"
  className: layout-box-hint
  frontmatterKey: layoutBoxHint
layout:
  position: afterBody
  priority: 30
  display: mobile-only
On narrow screens the explorer disappears behind a button. A sentence explaining that belongs exactly
where the problem occurs — and nowhere else.
The line in the footer
options:
  html: >-
    <p>{{siteTitle}} · Language: {{locale}} · This page:
    <code>{{slug}}</code></p>
  className: layout-box-colophon
layout:
  position: footer
  priority: 10
A colophon that writes itself: title, language and path all come from placeholders. On a site that
demonstrates its own machinery that is a sensible line — on one that has something else to say it is
ballast.


                  
                  Two languages means byLang
                  
                

As soon as a snippet holds text, the second language needs an entry of its own. The Example
template has seven boxes, four of them carrying text — and exactly those four appear twice in the
configuration.

en/layout-box/8-recipes/index.title: 8 – Recipes
en/layout-box/8-recipes/index.content:
Every recipe here is on this page. Anyone wanting to see what a box looks like before building it
scrolls up.

en/layout-box/9-reference/02-messages.title: 9.2 – Messages
en/layout-box/9-reference/02-messages.content:
Every message starts with [layout-box] and appears once per cause, not once per page. That is
deliberate: with 300 pages and one missing file, 300 identical lines would be no help.
Refusing to read "…" outside of "…"
The path in file leads out of dir. The box outputs nothing.
Usually one .. too many, or a dir that is not what you thought it was. See
2.2.
Snippet file not found: /full/path/to/file
There is no file at that place. The message names the full path — comparing it with where the
file actually is, is the fastest way to the cause.
Under --serve a dashed box appears on the page as well. In a normal build the spot stays empty.
Could not read snippet file (…)
The file is there but could not be read — permissions, a directory instead of a file, a broken
symlink. What the operating system reported is in the brackets. Otherwise it behaves like the
previous one: nothing in a normal build, a box under --serve.
`collapsible` requires a `title`; rendering non-collapsible
collapsible: true without a title. The box is rendered normally, only not collapsible. If the
cause sits in a byLang entry, the message names it.
It is produced while the instance is built, so it only ever sees the configuration. When
collapsible comes from a page’s frontmatter, the console stays silent and the box is quietly
rendered non-collapsible.
No message, no box
There are two causes for that, and neither is a fault:

The snippet is empty. A box without content outputs nothing — deliberately, see
6.2.
The page has hidden the box in its frontmatter.

When nothing at all happens
If the box is absent and the console is silent too, usually the entry itself is not in effect:
enabled: false, or the plugin is installed but not entered in quartz.config.yaml.
When the box sits somewhere else
An entry without a layout block still creates an instance. Quartz places any component that
names no position at its manifest’s default — for this plugin left, with priority: 15
(3.2). Removing the layout block to switch a box off therefore
puts it in the left column; enabled: false is what switches it off.

en/layout-box/9-reference/03-limits.title: 9.3 – Limits
en/layout-box/9-reference/03-limits.content:
It filters nothing
A snippet is inserted as it stands — as HTML, unchecked. That is the point: anyone wanting to insert
an <svg> or a <style> should be able to.
The consequence: only use files you control yourself. A snippet from a foreign source is as
trustworthy as foreign JavaScript. That does not apply to values from the page — placeholders are
escaped (4.1).
It knows no conditions
No expressions, no comparisons, no rules per folder. A page can hide a box or swap its snippet,
nothing more. Why, and what helps instead: 6.2.
It renders no Obsidian syntax
Wikilinks, callouts and embeds stay in a Markdown snippet as written. The plugin is a pure component
and sits behind the content pipeline
(1.3).
It remembers nothing in the browser
An opened box is back to whatever collapsed says after the next page change. Without JavaScript it
cannot be otherwise — and shipping no JavaScript is a decision, not a gap
(5.1).
The cache hangs on the modification time
Not on the content. Writing a file back with its old timestamp shows the old version. In practice
this only affects restoring from an archive.
Snippets are public
They live under quartz/static/ and are shipped along. They can be fetched through the site’s
address. For markup that appears on every page anyway that is of no consequence — as a place for
anything non-public the folder is unsuitable.
What is deliberately absent

No scheduling. No box that appears on Monday and disappears on Friday.
No template language. Placeholders insert values; they cannot calculate, branch or repeat.
No built-in styling. Apart from two rules for images the plugin brings no appearance with it
(5.2).

en/layout-box/index.title: Layout Box
en/layout-box/index.content:
quartz-layout-box puts a piece of HTML or Markdown anywhere in the Quartz layout: into a
sidebar, the header, the footer, before or after the page body. A word mark, a subtitle, a notice, a
call to action, a line stating where the page stands — anything meant to look the same across many
pages without being written into a theme.
What it does


                  
                  Anywhere on the page 
                  
                

Header, both sidebars, before and after the text, footer — and as often as you like: every entry
is a box of its own with its own options. → 3




                  
                  HTML or Markdown, from a file or straight from the configuration 
                  
                

A Markdown snippet is turned into HTML at build time. Kept as a file, a change shows in the
preview on the next reload, without a restart. → 2




                  
                  Placeholders 
                  
                

The page title, the site title, the page’s path, the way back to the start page and any
frontmatter field can be filled in — one box that says something different on every page. →
4




                  
                  Heading, collapsing, a class of its own 
                  
                

A box can carry a heading and collapse and expand, without any JavaScript. A class of its own is
what you style it by; images come in one variant per colour scheme. → 5




                  
                  Controllable per page 
                  
                

A single page hides the box through its frontmatter, or swaps the snippet and the heading. →
6




                  
                  Its own text in every language 
                  
                

With byLang every language gets its own file, its own text and its own heading — made to go
with quartz-multilanguage. →
7


The plugin works entirely at build time and ships no JavaScript to the browser.


                  
                  This site is its own evidence 
                  
                

It is built with the plugin. The word mark at the top left, the chapter name beside it and the box
at the bottom of the left column are three layout boxes; chapter 8 takes
each of them apart.


The nine chapters













































ChapterThe question it answers1 – Getting startedWhat is the plugin for, and how does the first box appear?2 – The snippetFile or configuration, HTML or Markdown?3 – PlacementWhere may a box sit, and in what order?4 – PlaceholdersHow does the page title get into the box?5 – FormHeading, collapsing, your own class — and how to style it6 – Per pageHow does a single page hide or swap the box?7 – Two languagesHow does each language get its own text?8 – RecipesFinished examples, all visible on this page9 – ReferenceEvery option, every message, the glossary
In one minute
npx quartz plugin add github:boxi-os/quartz-layout-box
Create a snippet at quartz/static/snippets/snippet.html, add the entry to quartz.config.yaml,
done:
plugins:
  - source: github:boxi-os/quartz-layout-box
    enabled: true
    options:
      file: snippet.html
    layout:
      position: left
      priority: 15
At length under 1.2 – Your first box.
Where else it is written
The short version is the repository README — the
same options, without examples. The plugin belongs to
QuartzControl, where it can be set up without writing
YAML; the app is not required, though.
Licence
quartz-layout-box is under the MIT licence.

en/multilanguage/1-getting-started/01-wh.title: 1.1 – What Quartz can do alone
en/multilanguage/1-getting-started/01-wh.content:
There is one field in quartz.config.yaml:
configuration:
  locale: en-US
It decides the interface: the words Quartz contributes itself — “Backlinks”, “Last updated”, the
label on the search — and the format of dates. It applies to the whole site, and there is exactly
one of it.
That is enough to build a site in one language. Anyone with notes in two languages can put them
all in one vault — Quartz builds pages from them, and the pages sit next to each other. What is
missing is everything that turns two piles of pages into one bilingual site:

































What is missingWhat that meansThe language per pageQuartz does not know that de/kaffee is German. <html lang> says the same on every page.The connectionNobody knows that de/kaffee and en/coffee are the same page.A switcherWithout the connection there cannot be one.hreflangSearch engines see two independent pages instead of two versions of one.The way in/ leads to a start page. Which one?The noticeA visitor lands in the wrong language and never learns that theirs exists.
Those six gaps are exactly what the plugin fills — each in a chapter of this handbook.
What it does not change
The site-wide locale stays. The interface texts of other plugins still follow it, not the
language of the individual page. On an English site the box under the text therefore says
“Backlinks” on the German pages too.
That is not negligence but the line between plugin and Quartz: those texts come from Quartz’ own
translation table, which is loaded once per build. Anyone wanting them translated as well builds
one site per language — how, is in chapter 8.

en/multilanguage/1-getting-started/02-yo.title: 1.2 – Your first bilingual site
en/multilanguage/1-getting-started/02-yo.content:
1. Order the content
The simplest way is two language folders:
content/
  de/
    index.md
    kaffee.md
  en/
    index.md
    coffee.md

Other ways — file suffixes, a frontmatter field — are in chapter 2.
2. Install the plugin
npx quartz plugin add github:boxi-os/quartz-multilanguage
3. Add the entry
plugins:
  - source: github:boxi-os/quartz-multilanguage
    enabled: true
    order: 65
    options:
      languages:
        - { code: de, native: Deutsch, locale: de-DE }
        - { code: en, native: English, locale: en-US }
      defaultLanguage: de
    layout:
      position: header
      group: toolbar
One entry is enough. The plugin is several things at once — what, is under
1.3; the configuration notices none of it.
4. Look at it
npx quartz build --serve
The switcher sits at the top right. A click leads from de/kaffee to en/coffee — provided the two
are linked. With identical base paths that happens by itself; de/kaffee and en/coffee are named
differently, though, and that needs a hint in the frontmatter:
---
title: Kaffee
translationKey: kaffee
---
The same line in en/coffee.md, and the two belong together.
Chapter 3 shows the three ways there.
When something is off

























What you seeWhat causes itNo switcherOnly one language configured — or the page has no translation and switcher.missing: hide is set.The switcher goes to the start pageThe pages are not linked. That is the normal case with missing: home.Every page counts as Germandetection finds nothing — check the folder names, or defaultLanguage.<html lang> is wronglocale is missing from the language entry; without it the code is used.

en/multilanguage/1-getting-started/03-th.title: 1.3 – The six parts
en/multilanguage/1-getting-started/03-th.content:
One entry in the configuration, but six roles in the build. Knowing which runs when explains most of
the plugin’s quirks by itself.








































RoleWhenWhat it doesTransformerwhile processing each pagedetects the language, sets frontmatter.lang and fileData.multilanguageLinkingafter all pages are readgroups translations with one anotherFilterbefore renderingremoves languages that are not being published (chapter 8)Emitterwhile writingcreates the redirect pages, the root index.html and static/multilanguage.json for the scriptComponentwhile building the layoutrenders the switcherScriptin the browsernotices, remembered language choice, localized dates, breadcrumbs
Why the linking comes afterwards
A transformer only ever sees one page. Whether de/kaffee has an English version can only be
said once every page has been read — which is why the grouping happens in a step of its own after
that.
Something practical follows from it: a page removed from the build by a filter — a draft, an
unlisted page — is not there for the linking either. The switcher then does not show it.
For the switcher that always holds, because it reads the list after every filter. For hreflang
it depends on the order the filters run in among themselves — see the second box below.
Why order almost never matters
order sets the order of the transformers. For language detection it is almost irrelevant — it only
needs the frontmatter, which note-properties (order 5) has long since read.


                  
                  The one exception, for the transformer 
                  
                

rewriteCrossLanguageLinks reads the data-slug that crawl-links (order 60) leaves on every
link while resolving it. The rewriting therefore has to run after crawl-links, and
order: 65 does exactly that. Put the plugin earlier and you get no message — you get links that
silently stay uncorrected. Anyone not using that option may leave the line out.




                  
                  And a second one, for the filter 
                  
                

order applies to this plugin’s filter too, not only to its transformer — and that filter has
two jobs: it removes languages that are not published and records every page it lets through in
the list hreflang later draws from. Below 50, that is before remove-draft, it records drafts
before they are removed; the hreflang of a published page then names an address that does not
exist, and nobody sees it. Measured: at order: 40 the draft appears in hreflang, at order: 65
it does not. The switcher is unaffected.


The script
Three things happen only in the browser, because they concern the visitor rather than the page: the
notices about translations (chapter 7), remembering the language choice and
formatting the dates.
A fourth, because it belongs to another plugin: the breadcrumbs of @quartz-community/breadcrumbs
always start at the root of the site, with one name for all languages there. The script makes them
start at the home page of the page’s language and calls it “Home” or “Start”; pages of the default
language keep a rootName of your own. On the home page of a language they disappear, as on the
root one.
Everything else happens at build time. Without JavaScript the switcher, hreflang and the redirects
keep working — only those four things do not.

en/multilanguage/2-detection/01-the-thre.title: 2.1 – The three ways
en/multilanguage/2-detection/01-the-thre.content:
Language folders
content/de/notizen/kaffee.md      → language de, base path notizen/kaffee
content/en/notes/coffee.md        → language en, base path notes/coffee

The usual way, and the one with the fewest surprises: the page’s address carries the language
visibly, redirects and link rewriting work, and the languages sit apart in the vault.
File suffix
content/guide.md                  → default language, base path guide
content/guide.de.md               → language de, base path guide

Good for sites where only part is translated: the two versions sit side by side, and deleting the
German one changes nothing about the English. The price is an address that does not show its
language.
Frontmatter
---
title: Mentions légales
lang: fr
---
For individual cases that fit no convention — a French imprint on an otherwise bilingual site.


                  
                  The way with the most restrictions 
                  
                

A page detected only through the frontmatter has no slug convention: from its path there is no
way to derive what its translation would be called. Fallback redirects
(chapter 6) and link rewriting
(7.2) therefore do not apply to it. The switcher and
hreflang do.


Combining is the normal case
All three may sit side by side. A site with language folders can assign a single file to a third
language through the frontmatter without creating a folder for it.

en/multilanguage/2-detection/02-order-an.title: 2.2 – Order and base path
en/multilanguage/2-detection/02-order-an.content:
options:
  detection: [folder, suffix, frontmatter]   # default
  defaultLanguage: de
They are tried in that order, and the first match wins. A file de/guide.en.md therefore belongs
to de when folder comes before suffix — the folder was there first.
Turning that around turns the result around:
options:
  detection: [suffix, folder, frontmatter]
An empty list (detection: []) assigns everything to the default language. That is not an
accident but the way to switch detection off and link everything by hand through translations.
When nothing matches
Then defaultLanguage applies. Without one that is the first language in languages — an order
easily overlooked when a language is later moved to the front.
The base path
Every detection yields not only the language but also the base path: the slug without the
language part.






























FileLanguageBase pathde/notizen/kaffee.mddenotizen/kaffeeen/notizen/kaffee.mdennotizen/kaffeeguide.de.mddeguideguide.mden (default)guide
It is the thing that really matters, because three things rest on it: the tacit linking through
identical paths (chapter 3), the fallback redirects and the link rewriting.


                  
                  Identical base paths save all configuration 
                  
                

Anyone naming their files the same in both languages — de/notizen/kaffee and
en/notizen/kaffee — needs no translationKey and no translations. The link follows by itself.
Only translated file names (en/notes/coffee) have to be spelled out.


What every page carries afterwards
fileData.multilanguage = {
  lang, baseSlug, source, translationKey, translations
}

source says which of the three ways applied — useful when a page unexpectedly ends up in the wrong
language. In addition frontmatter.lang is set if it is missing; Quartz makes <html lang> out of
it.

en/multilanguage/3-linking/01-the-three-.title: 3.1 – The three strategies
en/multilanguage/3-linking/01-the-three-.content:
options:
  linking: [frontmatter, aliases, path]   # default
As with detection: tried in that order, the first match wins.
Frontmatter
Two spellings. The shorter one is a shared key on both pages:
---
title: Kaffee
translationKey: kaffee
---
The fuller one names the partners directly — useful when only one page should be touched:
---
title: Kaffee
translations:
  en: en/notes/coffee
---
Wikilinks are allowed there: en: "[[en/notes/coffee]]".
Aliases
If a page carries an alias matching the title or file name of a page in another language, the two
count as translations:
---
title: Kaffee
aliases: [Coffee]
---
That is exactly what the Obsidian plugin
Multilingual writes: it stores translated note
names as ordinary aliases. Anyone working with it gets the linking for free.
Together with switcher.label: translatedTitle the switcher then says “Coffee” on the German page
and “Kaffee” on the English one.
Path
Same base path, different language — done. de/notizen/kaffee and en/notizen/kaffee find each
other with no declaration at all, and so do guide.md and guide.de.md.
The quietest way, and for sites that do not translate their file names the only one needed.
The precedence
If a page holds a translationKey and a path matched at the same time, the frontmatter wins — it is
the explicit statement. Which is why frontmatter comes first in the default.
Changing the order changes which statement counts in case of doubt:
options:
  linking: [path, frontmatter]   # the path beats the frontmatter

en/multilanguage/3-linking/02-when-it-do.title: 3.2 – When it does not work
en/multilanguage/3-linking/02-when-it-do.content:
Never two pages of one language
A group of translations holds at most one page per language. If two German pages carry the same
translationKey, that is a contradiction: the plugin skips the link and warns at build time.
That happens more often than one would think — when a key travels along with a copied page, for
instance.
Filtered pages are not there
The linking runs after the build’s filters have run. A page with draft: true, an unlisted one, or
one removed by publishLanguages does not exist for the switcher — it does not show it.


                  
                  That is correct, and it looks like a bug 
                  
                

Writing a translation, marking it as a draft and then wondering why the switcher does not know it
means looking for the fault in the wrong place.




                  
                  For hreflang it only holds at the default order
                  
                

The switcher reads the list after every filter, so a draft is always missing there. hreflang
draws from a list this plugin’s own filter fills — and a filter running after it removes pages
that are already recorded. With the defaults the order is right; set order below 50 and drafts
turn up in hreflang (1.3).


Seeing what was found
Every page carries the result with it:
fileData.multilanguage = {
  lang: "de",
  baseSlug: "notizen/kaffee",
  source: "folder",
  translationKey: "kaffee",
  translations: { en: "en/notes/coffee" }
}

The same thing sits in the built HTML on the switcher as data-translations — the fastest way to
look without changing anything: open the page, inspect the element.
If source shows a different way than expected, the fault is in the detection
(2.2), not in the linking.
The most common causes

























ObservationCauseSwitcher goes to the start pageNo link found — with switcher.missing: home the normal caseSwitcher does not show the language at allswitcher.missing: hideTwo pages link up wronglyIdentical base paths where no translation was meant — restrict linking or renameThe link seems to work one way onlyIt is always mutual; if it looks one-sided, these are two separate groups

en/multilanguage/3-linking/index.title: 3 – Linking
en/multilanguage/3-linking/index.content:
The language is detected; now de/kaffee has to learn that en/coffee exists.

en/multilanguage/4-switcher/01-form-and-.title: 4.1 – Form and labels
en/multilanguage/4-switcher/01-form-and-.content:
options:
  switcher:
    style: dropdown
    label: native
    showCurrent: true
    separator: "|"
Three shapes

























styleWhat it isWhat forlinkstext links side by side, parted by separatortwo, at most three languagesdropdowna details element to openmany languages, or little roomflagsthe flag field per language, native name as a tooltipwhen room is tight and the languages are known
dropdown works without JavaScript — it is a details. The plugin’s script additionally closes
it on a click outside and on Escape; without the script, opening still works.
The switcher at the top right of this site is a dropdown with label: native.


                  
                  Flags are countries, not languages 
                  
                

A country can have several languages, a language several countries. Which flag stands for English?
Anyone choosing flags should know the choice always passes somebody over. The default derives the
flag from the locale’s region (de-DE → 🇩🇪); the flag field overrides any of them, with text if
you like.


Four labels






























labelShowsExamplecodethe language codedelabelthe display nameGermannativethe name in the language itselfDeutschtranslatedTitlethe title of the target pageKaffee
native is usually the friendliest choice: someone looking for German is looking for “Deutsch”, not
“German”.
translatedTitle is the most interesting — it shows where the click leads, not just into which
language. It needs a link that knows the title; without a translation it falls back to the native
name.
The current language
showCurrent: true shows it as a highlighted entry without a link, carrying aria-current="page".
With false only the others appear — shorter, but the visitor no longer sees where they are.
Where it belongs
layout:
  position: header
  group: toolbar
Next to the search and the colour-scheme button, where visitors look for such switches. Any other
place works too — the values are the same as for any Quartz component.
On a monolingual site, and on pages with no further entries, it renders nothing. So no condition
is needed around it.

en/multilanguage/4-switcher/02-missing-t.title: 4.2 – Missing translations
en/multilanguage/4-switcher/02-missing-t.content:
The normal case on a growing site: the page exists in English, the German one is still missing. What
should the switcher say?
options:
  switcher:
    missing: home

























missingWhat happensPricehomeThe entry leads to that language’s start pageThe click goes somewhere other than expected — the tooltip says so, but not everyone reads ithideThe entry is absentThe switcher changes length from page to page, and nobody learns the language existsdisabledThe entry is there, greyed out, without a linkHonest, but a dead entry taking up room
The default is home — at least it leads to where the language begins.
What the switcher emits for it
A fallback entry gets a class of its own and a tooltip:
<a href="../fr/" class="fallback" hreflang="fr-FR" lang="fr-FR"
   data-lang="fr" title="Français (start page)">Français</a>
Through .multilanguage-switcher .fallback it can be set apart in the site’s CSS — italic, paler,
with a mark after it. That takes the sting out of home without making the entry disappear.
The alternative: redirects
If home is too vague, you can instead make sure the address exists at all: fallbackPages: redirect creates a redirect page for every missing translation, leading to the version that does
exist. The click then goes to de/coffee, lands on en/coffee, and the address works as a bookmark
too. See 6.2 – Missing pages.
And the notice
The other way round: when a visitor lands on the English page although they speak German, and the
German version exists — they should learn about it without searching the switcher. That is what the
notices in chapter 7 are for.

en/multilanguage/5-addresses/01-hreflang.title: 5.1 – hreflang and x-default
en/multilanguage/5-addresses/01-hreflang.content:
Without the hint a search engine sees two independent pages with similar content. With hreflang it
sees two versions of one page and shows each searcher the one in their language.
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="de-DE" href="example.org/de/notizen/kaffee" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-US" href="example.org/en/notes/coffee" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="example.org/en/notes/coffee" />
options:
  seo:
    hreflang: true      # default
    xDefault: default


                  
                  No baseUrl, no hreflang
                  
                

The declaration requires absolute addresses. With no baseUrl in the Quartz configuration the
plugin leaves the lines out — it has nothing to build them from. That is the most common reason
they are missing.


x-default
Says which version should apply when no language fits.





















ValueMeaningdefaultthe site’s default language (default)noneno declarationa language codeexactly that language
For a site whose English version is the more complete one, xDefault: en makes sense even when the
default language is German.
What gets linked
Only pages that have a link (chapter 3) and that survived the build. With
the folder and suffix conventions the plugin can derive the partners from the slugs if the grouping
found nothing.
A page without translations gets no hreflang lines — there is nothing to link.

en/multilanguage/5-addresses/02-og-local.title: 5.2 – og:locale and html lang
en/multilanguage/5-addresses/02-og-local.content:
og:locale
<meta property="og:locale" content="de_DE" />
<meta property="og:locale:alternate" content="en_US" />
What social networks read when somebody shares a link. Switched off with seo.ogLocale: false.
Note the underscore: Open Graph writes de_DE, hreflang writes de-DE. The plugin sets both
correctly from the same locale field.
<html lang>
That is produced by Quartz, not by the plugin — from the page’s frontmatter field lang. And
that field is exactly what the plugin sets during detection, if it is missing.
A small chain follows:
folder name de/  →  detection  →  frontmatter.lang = de-DE  →  <html lang="de-DE">

Writing the field yourself does not get overridden by the detection — it is only set when absent.
code and locale are two things




















FieldWhat forExamplecodefolder names, file suffixes, frontmatter, data-langdelocale<html lang>, hreflang, og:localede-DE
Without a locale the plugin takes the code — then <html lang="de"> appears. That is valid but
less precise: de-AT and de-DE differ in date and number formats.
languages:
  - { code: de, native: Deutsch, locale: de-DE }
  - { code: en, native: English, locale: en-US }


                  
                  Why screen reader users notice 
                  
                

<html lang> decides which pronunciation a screen reader uses. With the wrong language there,
German text is read out in English — incomprehensible, and this is the cheapest accessibility
improvement there is.

en/multilanguage/6-redirects/01-the-star.title: 6.1 – The start page
en/multilanguage/6-redirects/01-the-star.content:
Anyone maintaining de/index.md and en/index.md has nothing at /. The plugin writes a small
index.html there that redirects:
options:
  rootRedirect: browser
  rememberChoice: true





















rootRedirectWhat happensnonenothing (default)defaultalways to the default language’s start pagebrowserto the visitor’s language, if one fits


                  
                  Only when the root is free 
                  
                

If an index.md sits directly in the vault, / belongs to it. The plugin does not overwrite it.


How browser decides
In order:

The remembered choice — if the visitor has picked a language in the switcher before, that
applies.
navigator.languages — the browser’s languages, in its order; the first match among the
configured ones wins.
The default language.

The remembered choice comes first, and that is the point: somebody who once switched to German does
not want to land in English on the next visit just because their browser says so.
Switched off with rememberChoice: false — then only the browser language remains.
Without JavaScript
The generated page contains both: a <noscript> with a meta refresh to the default language and a
plain list of all language links. Whoever arrives without a script is redirected or can click; the
page is never empty.


                  
                  Redirects are no substitute for content, as far as search engines go 
                  
                

A root that only redirects has nothing to index. Anyone who cares about the start page is better
off maintaining a real index.md with hreflang to the language versions.

en/multilanguage/6-redirects/02-missing-.title: 6.2 – Missing pages
en/multilanguage/6-redirects/02-missing-.content:
en/notes/coffee exists, de/notes/coffee does not. A link to it — from an email, a bookmark,
another site — leads nowhere.
options:
  fallbackPages: redirect
With that the plugin writes de/notes/coffee.html with a redirect to the English version. The
address works, and the visitor arrives at the content. The file is named after the slug plus .html
— not a directory with an index.html inside it; look for it in the built folder under the other
name and you look in the wrong place.
The generated pages carry noindex — they are not meant to appear in search results themselves, only
to keep addresses alive.
Folder and suffix conventions only
Both procedures rest on computing the other language’s slug from one: en/notes/coffee →
de/notes/coffee. For a page whose language sits only in the frontmatter that computation does not
exist — no redirect is created for it (2.1).
Folder pages are exempt
No redirect is written for a folder’s index page. The reason is concrete: Quartz creates a page
for every folder listing its contents, and a redirect in the same place would overwrite it. A useful
listing would turn into a jump into the other language.
When this is not the right answer
Redirects are good for addresses that once existed or that somebody might guess. For a site that is
deliberately only partly translated they are a quiet way of hiding the state: every click lands in
the other language, and nobody sees how much is missing.
The more honest combination there is switcher.missing: disabled — the entry is there, greyed out,
telling the truth.
