en/multilanguage/7-notices/01-the-two-no.title: 7.1 – The two notices
en/multilanguage/7-notices/01-the-two-no.content:
options:
  missingTranslationNotice: true
  availableTranslationNotice: true




















OptionWhen the sentence appearsWhat it saysmissingTranslationNoticeThe visitor speaks a language this page does not exist in“This page is only available in English.”availableTranslationNoticeIt also exists in their language“This page is also available in German.” — with a link
The second is the more important one: it catches the visitor who arrived in the wrong language
through a search engine. This site has it switched on; on a German page with an English browser it
sits above the text.
Why this is decided in the browser
Which language somebody prefers is known only to their browser. At build time it is not known, and a
page cannot be shipped in two versions at once.
The plugin therefore puts an empty, hidden callout at the top of every page. The script compares
the page’s language with the visitor’s preferred one — remembered choice, else browser language —
and fills in the matching text. If nothing matches, the box stays empty and invisible.


                  
                  The text is in the visitor's language 
                  
                

Somebody who speaks German and lands on an English page reads “Diese Seite gibt es auch auf
Deutsch” — in German. That is the point: the sentence addresses somebody who may not read the
page’s language.


The plugin carries the texts for en-US, de-DE, fr-FR and es-ES; other languages fall back to
English.
Why they never reach the search index
Because the box is empty at build time. The text comes into being in the browser and therefore
reaches neither the page description nor the search index. Both would otherwise be polluted with a
sentence that is not part of the content at all.
Appearance
The box carries the class callout and so takes on the look of Obsidian callouts when that plugin is
active. Without it, it is a plain box that can be styled through .multilanguage-notice.

en/multilanguage/7-notices/02-links-betw.title: 7.2 – Links between languages
en/multilanguage/7-notices/02-links-betw.content:
Obsidian resolves [[coffee]] to the shortest matching path. In a bilingual vault that can be
the copy in the other language — a German page then links to en/notes/coffee although
de/notes/coffee exists.
In the vault that hardly shows. On the built site it throws the reader out of their language.
options:
  rewriteCrossLanguageLinks: true
order: 65
With that, such a link is rewritten at build time: to the version in the language of the linking
page, if it exists. If it does not, the link stays as it was — a jump into the other language beats a
jump into nothing.


                  
                  Here order matters
                  
                

The rewriting recognises a link by the data-slug that crawl-links (order 60) gave it while
resolving it. It therefore has to happen after crawl-links — hence order: 65, the higher
number running later. With the plugin earlier there is no data-slug to find, the rewriting comes
to nothing and nobody notices: the links stay quietly wrong.


Folder and suffix conventions only
As with the redirects, this rests on computing the other language’s slug from one. Pages whose
language sits only in the frontmatter are exempt.
Localized dates
options:
  localizeDates: true
Without this option every date follows the site-wide locale — on a German site the English pages
say 10. Sept. 2026.
With it, the script formats every <time datetime> element in the browser in the language of the
page, in the same format Quartz uses elsewhere.


                  
                  Why this too happens only in the browser 
                  
                

The formatting needs the reader’s time zone and regional settings. At build time there is neither —
what would appear is the date in the build machine’s time zone.

en/multilanguage/7-notices/index.title: 7 – Notices and links
en/multilanguage/7-notices/index.content:
Three things that concern the visitor and are therefore decided in the browser.

















PageContent7.1 – The two notices“only in English” and “also in German”7.2 – Links between languagesWhen Obsidian points at the wrong version

en/multilanguage/8-building/01-one-site-.title: 8.1 – One site for all
en/multilanguage/8-building/01-one-site-.content:
The normal case, and the one this site uses: one build, every language. One address, one deploy,
one search, and the switcher jumps between the versions without a detour.
What works properly:

Switcher, hreflang, redirects, notices — all of them know all languages
A link from a German to an English page stays an ordinary link
The explorer shows both language trees

The one place where it grates
The interface texts follow the site-wide locale: “Backlinks”, “Last updated”, the label on the
search, the date format. On a German site that is what the English pages say too.
Two things help without splitting the build:

localizeDates: true — at least the dates then follow the page’s language
(7.2).
Filter the explorer — it can show one tree per language. The helper for that is in
9.2.

For everything else: anyone needing a fully translated interface builds once per language —
8.2.
The search index covers every language
A search for “coffee” also finds the German page if the word appears there. That is rarely a problem
and sometimes wanted; in a shared build it cannot be turned off.

en/multilanguage/8-building/02-one-build.title: 8.2 – One build per language
en/multilanguage/8-building/02-one-build.content:
options:
  publishLanguages: [de]
Or, without touching the configuration:
QUARTZ_LANGS=de npx quartz build
The environment variable overrides the option. Every other language is removed before rendering;
switcher, hreflang, redirects and notices then know only what is being published.
What that gains
Combined with a quartz.config.yaml of its own per build — a different locale, a different
baseUrl — a fully localized site comes out: “Backlinks”, “Last updated” and the date format are
right too, because they follow the site-wide locale and that now fits.
QUARTZ_LANGS=de npx quartz build --output public-de
QUARTZ_LANGS=en npx quartz build --output public-en
Two folders, two deploys, two addresses — example.org and example.org/en, say, or two domains.
What it costs



































One buildOne build per languageInterface textssite-wide, one languageright on each siteSearchevery language in one indexseparate per languageSwitcherjumps straight to the translationgoneDeployoneone per languageMaintenanceone configurationone per language
The third point is the one that surprises: two separate sites know nothing of each other, and the
plugin does not bridge that. With one published language the switcher component renders nothing at
all — it needs two active languages — and hreflang stays empty for the same reason. To point from
one site at the other, place that link yourself, in the layout’s header for instance.


                  
                  Only when it is needed 
                  
                

One build is simpler, and most sites manage with it. The point where that turns is usually the one
where readers trip over interface texts in the wrong language — not the one where somebody
discovers the possibility.

en/multilanguage/9-reference/02-explorer.title: 9.2 – Explorer and Quartz
en/multilanguage/9-reference/02-explorer.content:
Filtering the explorer
Left alone, the explorer shows both language trees. Anyone wanting one per language needs a
filter function — and the explorer plugin takes one only through quartz.ts, not through
quartz.config.yaml.
// quartz.ts
import { languageExplorerFilter } from "./.quartz/plugins/quartz-multilanguage";
 
Explorer({ filterFn: languageExplorerFilter("de", { languages: ["de", "en"] }) });


                  
                  Why this cannot go in the configuration 
                  
                

YAML cannot hold a function. Anything Quartz takes as a function has to go through quartz.ts —
that is a property of Quartz, not a decision of this plugin.


Where the line runs

































The pluginQuartzdetects the language per pagerenders <html lang> from itlinks translationsknows nothing about themrenders the switcherprovides the place in the layoutwrites hreflang and og:localewrites the rest of the headfilters languages out of the buildbuilds what remains—translates its own interface texts according to locale
The last line is where most questions hang: what Quartz contributes in words follows the site-wide
locale, not the page’s language. That is not a gap in the plugin but the place where its remit
ends — the way out is one build per language
(8.2).
What every page carries
fileData.multilanguage = { lang, baseSlug, source, translationKey, translations }

Anyone writing their own components finds everything the plugin knows about a page there.

en/multilanguage/9-reference/03-limits.title: 9.3 – Limits
en/multilanguage/9-reference/03-limits.content:
The interface stays monolingual
Explorer titles, “Backlinks”, the date in the header — they follow the site-wide locale. For a
fully translated interface: one build per language
(8.2).
The search index covers every language
In a shared build the search finds hits in any language. That cannot be separated per language —
again, only through separate builds.
Writing direction is site-wide
dir (right to left) belongs to the whole site in Quartz. The plugin does not change it per page;
for Arabic or Hebrew alongside a Latin-script language a build of its own is needed.
Frontmatter pages have no slug convention
A page whose language comes only from the frontmatter has no computable partner path. Fallback
redirects and link rewriting do not apply to it; the switcher and hreflang do
(2.1).
Never two pages of one language in a group
A contradictory link is skipped and reported, not guessed
(3.2).
Four things need JavaScript
The notices, the remembered language choice, localizeDates and the start of the breadcrumbs
(1.3). Everything else — switcher,
hreflang, redirects — is settled at build time and works without a script.
The plugin translates nothing
It orders, links and points. The text is written by whoever writes the note.

en/multilanguage/index.title: Multilanguage
en/multilanguage/index.content:
Quartz knows one language per site — one locale in the configuration, and that is that.
quartz-multilanguage adds everything missing to publish the same notes from one vault in several
languages: it detects each page’s language, finds the translations of one another, brings a
switcher, writes hreflang and og:locale, redirects the start page and tells a visitor when their
language exists.
What it does


                  
                  Detect every page's language 
                  
                

By the language folder (en/…), by a suffix in the file name (note.en.md) or by a frontmatter
field — in the order you set. → 2




                  
                  Find the translations of one another 
                  
                

Through a shared key in the frontmatter, through Obsidian aliases (compatible with the Obsidian
plugin “Multilingual”) or simply through the same path. → 3




                  
                  A switcher 
                  
                

As text links, as a drop-down without JavaScript or as flags; labelled with the language code,
the name, the native name or the title of the translation. It leads to the translation of this
page. → 4




                  
                  What search engines need to know 
                  
                

<html lang>, hreflang with x-default and og:locale are right on every page. →
5




                  
                  Visitors land in their language 
                  
                

The start page redirects by the browser’s language and remembers a choice. Where a translation
is missing there is a redirect or a notice “only available in German”, and dates appear in the
page’s language. → 6, 7




                  
                  One site for all languages, or one per language 
                  
                

The usual case is one build with every language. Anyone wanting an address of their own per
language builds only the ones needed. → 8




                  
                  This site is its own evidence 
                  
                

It exists in German and English, out of one vault, with this plugin. The switcher at the top right
is its component; change the language and you land on the translation of this page.


The nine chapters













































ChapterThe question it answers1 – Getting startedWhat Quartz does alone, and what is added here2 – DetectionHow does a page know which language it is in?3 – LinkingHow do two versions of one page find each other?4 – The switcherWhat the change looks like, and what it says5 – Addresses and metadataWhat search engines learn about the multilingualism6 – RedirectsWhere does / lead, and what happens when a translation is missing?7 – Notices and links“This page is also available in …” — and links that change language8 – BuildingOne site for all languages, or one per language?9 – ReferenceEvery option, every limit
In one minute
npx quartz plugin add github:boxi-os/quartz-multilanguage
One entry configures everything at once — detection, linking, switcher:
plugins:
  - source: github:boxi-os/quartz-multilanguage
    enabled: true
    order: 65
    options:
      languages:
        - { code: de, native: Deutsch, locale: de-DE }
        - { code: en, native: English, locale: en-US }
      defaultLanguage: de
    layout:
      position: header
      group: toolbar
At length under [[en/multilanguage/1-getting-started/02-your-first-bilingual-site|1.2 – Your first bilingual
site]].
Where else it is written
The short version is the repository README. The
sister plugin quartz-layout-box puts markup into the
layout and works well alongside this one; both belong to
QuartzControl, though the app is not required.
Licence
quartz-multilanguage is under the MIT licence.

en/navigations/1-getting-started/01-why-.title: 1.1 – Why this plugin
en/navigations/1-getting-started/01-why-.content:
What Quartz ships
The explorer shows the content folder as a tree in the sidebar, with collapsible folders it
remembers. For a digital garden that is exactly right: you see everything, and you find everything.
For a website with sections it is not enough. It knows one form, it always shows the whole
tree, and it appears once on the page. Four things many websites need cannot be built with it:

























What is missingWhat it is called hereA menu bar in the header whose entries open submenusvariant: dropdown or megaOnly the section you are reading in the sidebarscope: section”Previous” and “next” in reading order below the textvariant: pagerA sitemap in the footervariant: columns
And on a smartphone the menu bar should turn into something that fits in one hand — a menu behind a
burger button, for instance (mobile: offcanvas).
What this plugin does differently
One plugin, as many entries as you like. Every entry in quartz.config.yaml is a navigation of
its own with its own options. A website can carry a bar with the first level at the top, an
accordion with the current section on the left and a pager at the bottom — the same plugin three
times.
All of them read the same tree. It is built from the content folders at build time and computed
only once per build, however many navigations show it
(1.3).
The page has a say. Titles, order and visibility can be set in the configuration or in the
page’s own frontmatter — navOrder, navTitle, navHide, navIcon
(chapter 2).
What it does not do

It does not force you to replace the explorer. Both can sit side by side; they share no class
names and do not interfere. This website has replaced it all the same, with an accordion
(8.1).
It knows no links that are not in the content folder. A menu item “GitHub” or “Imprint on
another domain” is not a page and appears in no tree. Quartz’s footer or a
layout box is the place for those.
It does not search. Search stays Quartz’s own.

en/navigations/1-getting-started/02-your.title: 1.2 – Your first navigation
en/navigations/1-getting-started/02-your.content:
Three steps, and the navigation is there.
1. Install the plugin
npx quartz plugin add github:boxi-os/quartz-navigations
The command fetches the plugin and adds it to quartz.config.yaml — with every option and its
default value, as a tree in the left column (position: left, priority: 10). That is already
a working navigation. The long list may be shortened: whatever is not there, the plugin assumes as
its default.
In QuartzControl the same is done through the
marketplace.
2. Write the entry
A short entry for a menu bar in the header:
plugins:
  - source: github:boxi-os/quartz-navigations
    enabled: true
    options:
      variant: bar
      depth: 1
      mobile: offcanvas
    layout:
      position: header
      priority: 20

variant chooses the form — here a horizontal bar (chapter 4).
depth: 1 shows only the first folder level (3.2).
mobile: offcanvas turns it into a menu behind a burger button on smartphones
(chapter 6).
layout tells Quartz where the navigation goes. It is not part of the plugin but Quartz’s own
mechanism for every component. Without the block the navigation does not disappear: Quartz puts
it at the plugin’s default, left with priority: 10.

A second navigation is a second entry with the same source. More on that in
1.3.
3. Look
npx quartz build --serve
The bar sits in the header, the entry of the current page is highlighted, and every folder above it
carries the active-trail mark. Below the site’s mobile breakpoint
(6.2) the bar disappears behind a burger button.
When nothing appears





































What you seeWhat causes itNothing, on no page, no messageenabled: false.The navigation is on the left instead of where you wanted itThe layout block is missing or indented wrongly; the plugin’s default applies.Nothing on some pagesrootPath is set and the page lies outside it — that is hideOutsideRoot (3.2). Or scope finds no folder for this page (3.1).Nothing, but rootPath … is not a folder with visible pagesThe folder does not exist, or everything in it is hidden (9.2).A page is missing from the navigationDraft, unlisted, navHide or an exclude pattern (2.3).The order is wrong2.2 – Sorting.Folders and pages are called “index” or carry numbers2.1 – Titles and folder pages.

en/navigations/1-getting-started/03-what.title: 1.3 – What happens at build time
en/navigations/1-getting-started/03-what.content:
From entry to component
Quartz reads quartz.config.yaml and creates a component for every active entry — in the place
its layout block names, or without a block on the left with priority: 10. The plugin receives
the options exactly as they are written in the file and fills in everything missing from its own
defaults. A value it does not know — variant: vertikal, say — is replaced by the default and
reported once (9.2).
Two entries with identical options share one component in Quartz. That is harmless as long as
they sit in different places — except for element IDs, see
7.3.
From folder to tree
Quartz hands every component the list of all pages of the build. The tree is made from it:

Every page becomes a node. Its path (docs/setup) decides which folder it hangs in.
Every folder becomes a node whose link is the folder page — docs/index.
Hidden things drop out: tag pages, the 404 page, drafts, unlisted, navHide, exclude
(2.3).
Every node gets a title (2.1).
The children of every folder are sorted (2.2).
Empty folders drop out.

Folders can always be linked. Without an index.md, Quartz’s folder-page plugin creates the
folder page itself. It is in the same list and is treated like a real one — only its title comes
from the directory name.
One tree per build, not per navigation
The tree is computed once and then read by all navigations that share the tree-shaping options:
sorting, hiding, include/exclude, icons. Three entries that differ only in variant, scope or
depth cost one tree, not three. On a multilingual site it is one tree per language
(8.3).
One consequence is worth knowing: two navigations can place the same page differently if they
sort or hide differently. That is intended — a pager by date next to a sidebar in manual order is a
legitimate setup.
From tree and page to <nav>
For each page the navigation picks its part of the tree (chapter 3), marks
the current page with active and every folder above it with active-trail, and writes finished
HTML with relative links. Nothing is rebuilt in the browser. Switch JavaScript off and you get
the same navigation.
What the browser adds
One script — one for all navigations of the site — adds what HTML alone cannot do:





























WhatWhere it is neededRemember open folderspersistState (5.1)Open menus on hover, close them on Escape and on a click elsewheredropdown, mega, flyout (5.2)Redirect panels that would stick out of the window or a columnthe same threeHold the page still behind the mobile menu, Escapemobile: offcanvas (6.1)Navigate when an option is chosen in the jump menuselect, mobile: select
Stylesheet and script reach the site once, however many navigations are on it.

en/navigations/1-getting-started/index.title: 1 – Getting started
en/navigations/1-getting-started/index.content: PageContent1.1 – Why this pluginWhat the explorer does and where it stops1.2 – Your first navigationInstall, add the entry, look — and what goes wrong1.3 – What happens at build timeFrom folder to tree, from tree to <nav>

en/navigations/2-the-tree/01-titles-and-.title: 2.1 – Titles and folder pages
en/navigations/2-the-tree/01-titles-and-.content:
The title of a page
The plugin takes the first value it finds:

navTitle in the frontmatter
title in the frontmatter
the file name without .md — 01 First Steps, not the slug 01-first-steps
the last part of the slug

navTitle is for cases where the page title is too long for a navigation:
---
title: Installing on macOS, Linux and in containers
navTitle: Installation
---
The title of a folder
In the navigation a folder is a node whose link is its folder page (docs/index). Its title
comes from:

navTitle in its index.md
title in its index.md
the real directory name — 02 Guides, not 02-guides
the last part of the slug

If there is no index.md, Quartz’s folder-page plugin creates the folder page itself at build
time. The folder stays linkable; its title then comes from the directory name.


                  
                  Folder notes count as folder pages 
                  
                

A file named like its folder (docs/docs.md) and an _index.md already arrive in Quartz as
docs/index. For the plugin they are the same as an index.md.


A page and a folder with the same name
about.md next to a folder about/ gives two entries: the page about and the folder
about/index. To turn them into one, move the page into the folder as index.md.
Numbers in front of the name
Many vaults sort with numbers: 01 Getting started, 02 Guides. The number decides the order
(2.2) — in the title you usually do not want to see it.
options:
  stripNumericPrefix: true
This removes a leading number and the character after it — 01-, 01 , 01_, 01. — from the
title. The order stays, because it is read from the file or directory name, not from the title.


                  
                  It also hits titles from the frontmatter 
                  
                

The number is removed from every title that starts that way, not just from file names.
title: 1.2 – Your first navigation becomes 2 – Your first navigation: 1 is the number, .
the character after it. That is why this handbook does not switch the option on. The only
exception is navTitle — whatever is written there stays as it is.

en/navigations/2-the-tree/02-sorting.title: 2.2 – Sorting
en/navigations/2-the-tree/02-sorting.content:
What gets sorted is always the children of one folder among themselves. There are three methods:
options:
  sort: manual        # manual | alphabetical | date
  sortDirection: asc  # asc | desc
  foldersFirst: first # first | last | mixed
Folders first
Before any method comes foldersFirst: first puts folders before pages, last after them, mixed
sorts both together. Within the folders and within the pages the chosen method then applies.
manual — the cascade
The default. Four stages, each one only decides where the previous one was tied:






























StageSourceExample1the order list in the configurationorder: { docs: [intro, setup] }2navOrder in the frontmatternavOrder: 103the number in front of the file or directory name02 Setup.md4the titleSetup
Whoever has no value at a stage comes after everyone who has one. A page with navOrder therefore
comes before every page without — whatever number the other carries in its file name.
Without order, navOrder and numbers, the cascade gives an alphabetical order.
The order list
The order in one place instead of spread across many frontmatter blocks:
options:
  order:
    "": [docs, blog, about]      # the root
    docs: [intro, setup, faq]

The key is the folder path; "" is the root. docs, docs/, docs/index and docs.md mean the
same.
An entry is the last part of the slug (intro) or the file or directory name (01 Intro);
upper and lower case do not matter.
Whatever is not in the list follows after it, ordered by stages 2 to 4.
An entry that does not exist in the folder is reported once by the build
(9.2) — usually a typo or a renamed file.



                  
                   foldersFirst comes before the list
                  
                

With the default foldersFirst: first, folders come before pages even if the list says
otherwise. about in the example above is a page and therefore ends up after docs and blog,
wherever it is in the list. For the list alone to count, add foldersFirst: mixed.


navOrder
A number, smaller first. Decimals and negative values work, as does a number in quotes. In an
index.md, navOrder sets the position of the folder among its siblings. Tip: use steps of ten,
so something fits in between later.
Numbers
01 Intro, 02-setup, 3_faq, 4. Appendix — a number at the start, followed by -, _, . or a
space. The number is compared as a number, 10 comes after 9. Whether it stays visible in the
title is decided by stripNumericPrefix (2.1).
alphabetical
The title only. Compared naturally — Part 2 before Part 10 — and regardless of case or accents.
The language decides the order of letters. The plugin sorts with the locale from the
Quartz configuration: with de-DE, Ärger sits next to Apfel; with sv-SE, after Zebra. That
way every machine that builds the site sorts the same. On a multilingual site every tree sorts by its
language: with the site’s locale when it is the same language, otherwise with the language code
(8.3).
date
options:
  sort: date
  dateField: created    # created | modified | published
  sortDirection: desc   # newest first
The dates come from Quartz’s created-modified-date plugin; its configuration decides which date a
page has. Pages without a date come last; with equal dates the title decides.
The direction
sortDirection: desc reverses every stage, including the title. Missing values still stay at the
end: a blog with sort: date and desc lists undated posts after the dated ones, not before.
Two navigations, two orders
Every entry sorts on its own. A pager through the posts by date and a sidebar in manual order get
along — they then read two differently sorted trees
(1.3).

en/navigations/2-the-tree/03-hiding-and-.title: 2.3 – Hiding and selecting
en/navigations/2-the-tree/03-hiding-and-.content:
Hiding here means: not in the navigation. The page is still built and remains reachable through
its address, links and search. To not publish a page at all, use Quartz’s own means — draft,
ignorePatterns, explicit-publish.
What is missing by itself






























WhatOptionDefaultthe 404 page—always hiddenthe tags folder with the tag pageshideTagstruepages marked unlisted by the unlisted-pages pluginhideUnlistedtruedrafts, draft: truehideDraftstrue
hideDrafts only matters if drafts reach the build at all. With Quartz’s remove-draft plugin they
are gone before that.
navHide — the page decides
---
title: Imprint
navHide: true
---
In an index.md, navHide: true hides the whole folder, with everything in it. The field
understands true, false and the words yes/no.
include and exclude — the configuration decides
Patterns on slugs, that is on the path as it appears in the address — without .md, with hyphens
instead of spaces.
options:
  exclude:
    - private         # the folder private with everything in it
    - "drafts/**"     # everything below drafts
    - "*/archive"     # any page or folder archive one level deep





















CharacterMeaning*any number of characters within one path segment**any number of characters across path segments?exactly one character
A folder name hits the whole subtree. It is not just the slug itself that is tested but every
folder above it: docs matches docs/index, docs/setup and docs/guides/alpha.
include is the counterpart: if anything is listed there, only what matches stays. exclude is
checked first and wins.
options:
  include: [docs]   # a navigation for the documentation only


                  
                   docs/* takes the folder with it
                  
                

* matches every child of docs — including index, and through the folder check everything
below. Nothing is left, and the empty folder drops out. Hiding just the folder page
(exclude: ["docs/index"]), on the other hand, keeps the folder: it then links to its first page
(3.3).


Empty folders
Whatever is left after hiding gets tidied up:




















OptionDefaultEffecthideEmptyFolderstruefolders without visible children drop outkeepIndexOnlyFolderstrue… unless they have a folder page of their own
Because folder-page creates a page for every folder, a folder whose pages are all hidden stays with
the defaults — as a link to its folder page. If you do not want that, set
keepIndexOnlyFolders: false. The root never drops out.

en/navigations/2-the-tree/index.title: 2 – The tree
en/navigations/2-the-tree/index.content:
Every navigation shows part of the same tree. This chapter is about the tree itself — what is in it,
what it is called and in what order. Which part is shown is in chapter 3.





















PageContent2.1 – Titles and folder pagesWhere an entry gets its name, and what numbers do to it2.2 – SortingManual, alphabetical, by date — and the cascade behind it2.3 – Hiding and selectingWhat is left out by itself, navHide, include and exclude
The four frontmatter fields
A page can have a say in its own entry:






























FieldEffectIn an index.mdnavTitletitle in the navigation instead of titletitle of the foldernavOrdernumber for manual order, smaller firstposition of the folder among its siblingsnavHidetrue hides the pagehides the whole foldernavIconicon before the title (7.1)icon of the folder
The names can be changed with frontmatterKeys, for instance when a vault already uses order:
options:
  frontmatterKeys:
    order: order
    title: short

en/navigations/3-the-scope/01-rootpath-a.title: 3.1 – rootPath and scope
en/navigations/3-the-scope/01-rootpath-a.content:
Two options, two questions:

rootPath — from which folder does the navigation count at all? The default is the site root.
scope — which folder below it is shown, depending on the page you are on?

What is shown is always the children of the chosen folder, not the folder itself. To have it as a
header above, use showScopeRoot (3.2).
rootPath
options:
  rootPath: docs
The navigation starts at docs: its top level is guides, Intro and Setup. docs, docs/,
/docs/index and docs.md mean the same. If the folder does not exist — or everything in it is
hidden — the navigation stays empty, and the build says so once.
On pages outside rootPath, here blog/first-post, the navigation does not appear at all. That
is hideOutsideRoot (3.2).
scope

























scopeShown are the children of …root (default)rootPath — the same on every pagesectionthe first-level folder below rootPath that contains the pageparentthe folder that contains the pagecurrentthe folder that is the page — or, for an ordinary page, its folder
The difference between parent and current only shows on folder pages. Side by side, without
rootPath:















































Current pagerootsectionparentcurrentindex (start page)rootnothingrootrootdocs/indexrootdocsrootdocsdocs/02-setuprootdocsdocsdocsdocs/guides/indexrootdocsdocsdocs/guidesdocs/guides/alpharootdocsdocs/guidesdocs/guides
The table was checked against the plugin’s functions, not derived from the description.
When to use which

root for everything that looks the same on every page: menu bar, sitemap, explorer
replacement.
section for a sidebar that shows only the current section. The start page has no section, so
it stays empty there — the left column of this website shows exactly that.
parent for “this page’s neighbours”. On a folder page those are the neighbouring folders.
current for “what is in here”. On a folder page those are its children.

Together with rootPath
section counts the first level below rootPath. With rootPath: docs the section of
docs/guides/alpha is therefore docs/guides.
parent on the folder page of rootPath itself shows its children: the folder above would lie
outside, so the navigation takes rootPath.
Pages that are not in the tree
If the current page is hidden — tag page, navHide, an exclude pattern — or written in another
language than the tree, the tree does not know it.
Then:

















scopeResultrootThe navigation appears, just without a marked entry.section, parent, currentThe navigation does not appear — without a page there is no reference folder.
That is not a bug but a tool: a German chapter navigation with language: de does not contain the
English pages, and so no German navigation appears on English pages
(8.3).

en/navigations/3-the-scope/02-levels-and.title: 3.2 – Levels and headers
en/navigations/3-the-scope/02-levels-and.content:
depth — how deep
options:
  depth: 1   # 0 = unlimited (default)
Counted from the chosen folder (3.1): depth: 1 shows only
its children, depth: 2 their children too. Folders at the limit appear as a link without expanding.
The usual values:





























Wheredepthmenu bar bar1dropdown2 — first level in the bar, second in the menumega3 — bar, column headings, entriessitemap columns2sidebar tree, accordion0
depth also applies to select and pager: a pager with depth: 1 only pages through the first
level.
hideOutsideRoot — where it hides itself
Only effective with rootPath. With the default true, the navigation appears only on the folder
page of rootPath and on pages below it.
options:
  rootPath: docs
  hideOutsideRoot: false   # the docs navigation on the blog too
false is right for a footer sitemap that should show the same subtree everywhere. true is right
for anything that only makes sense in one section. One navigation per language needs no rootPath for
that (8.3).
showScopeRoot — a header
options:
  scope: section
  showScopeRoot: true
Above the list sits the shown folder itself, as a link. With scope: section that is the name of the
section — “1 – Getting started” above the pages of the first chapter, as on the right of this page.
Where the link points is decided by folderLink (3.3).
showHome — a “Home” entry
options:
  variant: bar
  depth: 1
  showHome: true
The first entry of the list leads to the folder page of rootPath, without rootPath to the start
page. It is labelled “Home” (or “Start”, depending on the language — 7.3), in the vertical variants
with a house in front. It only appears if that page exists, and never with tabs.
indexEntry — an “Overview” row
options:
  variant: accordion
  indexEntry: first
Every folder whose children are shown and which has a folder page gets the entry “Overview” as its
first child, leading to that page.
This is needed when the folder row itself is not a link: with the default folderClick: toggle
a click on the row only expands the folder (5.1). Without
indexEntry the folder page would then be unreachable from this navigation.

en/navigations/3-the-scope/03-where-fold.title: 3.3 – Where folders link
en/navigations/3-the-scope/03-where-fold.content:
options:
  folderLink: index   # index | first-child | none





















ValueA folder title leads to …index (default)its folder page; if there is none, its first pagefirst-childits first page, even if it has a folder pagenonenothing — the title is text
The first page
“First page” means: the first entry in tree order (2.2) that is a page.
If a subfolder is there, the plugin keeps looking inside it — unless it has a folder page of its own,
in which case that is the first page.
first-child suits folders that are only structure: a click on “Guides” lands directly on the first
guide instead of an overview that has nothing to say.
Are there folders without a page at all?
Rarely. Quartz’s folder-page plugin creates a page for every folder, even without index.md. The
fallback of index to the first page only applies when folder-page is switched off — or when the
folder page was hidden, for instance with exclude: ["docs/index"].
What the other variants make of it





















VariantFolder without link target (none)lists, bars, menustitle as textselectoption cannot be selectedpagerskipped
And one peculiarity of the pager: if a folder and its first page lead to the same address, it
pages there only once. A “Previous” that points at the page you are on does not exist.
Folders that expand
In accordion, flyout, dropdown and mega a folder is more than a title — it expands. Whether
its row then expands or links is decided by a second option, folderClick
(5.1). folderLink only says where a link leads, if there is
one.

en/navigations/3-the-scope/index.title: 3 – The scope
en/navigations/3-the-scope/index.content:
A bar in the header shows the first level of the whole site, a sidebar only the section you are
reading. Both read the same tree (chapter 2) — they just pick different
parts of it.





















PageContent3.1 – rootPath and scopeFrom which folder, and relative to the current page3.2 – Levels and headersdepth, hideOutsideRoot, showScopeRoot, showHome, indexEntry3.3 – Where folders linkFolder page, first page or no link at all
The examples in this chapter assume this site:
index.md
blog/
  first-post.md
docs/
  index.md
  01 Intro.md
  02 Setup.md
  guides/
    alpha.md
    beta.md

en/navigations/4-variants/01-vertical.title: 4.1 – Vertical
en/navigations/4-variants/01-vertical.content:
The three vertical variants carry a glyph on every row, like a file explorer: a folder, an open
folder, a page (7.1). Folder rows get smaller and lighter with each
level, so you can find where a branch begins.
tree
options:
  variant: tree
A nested list, everything visible. Nothing expands, nothing opens; a thin line guides the eye down
the levels. The current page gets a background colour and an accent bar.
Right when the scope is small — one chapter, one section. The right column of this website is a
tree with scope: section.
accordion
options:
  variant: accordion
  expandActive: true         # default: the path to the current page is open
  folderDefaultState: collapsed
  persistState: true         # remember open folders
The same list, but every folder can be expanded. It is built with <details> and <summary> — so it
works without JavaScript too. The path to the current page is open, everything else closed until you
open it.
Right for a whole site in the sidebar — the obvious replacement for the explorer. What a click on a
folder row does, and how to keep only one folder per level open, is in
5.1.
flyout
options:
  variant: flyout
  trigger: hover     # or click (default)
  flyout:
    side: auto       # auto | right | left
A list whose folders do not expand downwards but open a panel beside them — like an operating
system menu. Deeper folders open their panel beside again.
Which side: with side: auto the browser decides when opening. If the navigation sits in the right
half of the page, the panels open to the left, otherwise to the right. right and left fix it.
Right when a sidebar should stay narrow and the tree is deep.


                  
                  Panels in a column that scrolls 
                  
                

Sidebars often scroll on their own (overflow: auto) or fade out softly at the bottom. A panel
inside would be cut off. The script therefore lifts it out of the column when it opens and anchors
it to its row; when the column scrolls, it closes (5.2).


Which of the three?





















QuestionAnswerShould everything be visible at a glance?treeIs the tree large but the column tall?accordionIs the column narrow and the tree deep?flyout

en/navigations/4-variants/02-horizontal.title: 4.2 – Horizontal
en/navigations/4-variants/02-horizontal.content:
The four horizontal variants put the first level into a row. They differ in what happens to the
levels below. The row itself has no glyphs, and all entries are the same size.
bar
options:
  variant: bar
  depth: 1
A row of links. With depth: 1 that is the classic menu bar. If deeper levels are allowed, they sit
in the same row behind their folder, whose name then gets a colon. That works for two levels with
few entries, in a footer for instance; for more there is dropdown.
dropdown
options:
  variant: dropdown
  depth: 2
  trigger: click   # or hover
The first level in the row; a folder opens a menu below with its children. Deeper levels are
indented in the same menu. Pages on the first level are ordinary links.
A menu that would stick out of the window on the right is hung from the right edge of its entry by the
script. Opening one closes the other; Escape and a click elsewhere close all
(5.2).
mega
options:
  variant: mega
  depth: 3
  trigger: hover
  folderClick: link
Like dropdown, but the menu is wide and split into columns: the second level forms the column
headings, the third sits below them. Right for large sites with sections that each have several
subsections. The width is set by --quartz-nav-mega-min-width (7.2).
tabs
options:
  variant: tabs
  tabs:
    secondary: true   # default
The first level as tabs. If the current page lies in a first-level folder, its children appear in
a second row below. With secondary: false it stays at the tab row.
Right for sites with a few large sections between which you rarely switch. There is no showHome for
tabs — the tab row has no place for it.
align — aligning the row
options:
  align: center   # left (default) | center | right | full

























ValueResultleftentries at the startcenterentries in the middlerightentries at the endfullevery entry gets an equal share of the width
Applies only to bar, dropdown, mega and tabs; the other variants ignore the option. With
mobile: accordion or offcanvas the entries stack below the mobile breakpoint and the alignment
no longer applies; with the default mobile: same the row just wraps (chapter 6).
Which of the four?

























QuestionAnswerOnly the sections, no subpages?bar with depth: 1Sections with a handful of pages?dropdownSections with subsections?megaA few sections, and you should see which one you are in?tabs

en/navigations/4-variants/03-special-for.title: 4.3 – Special forms
en/navigations/4-variants/03-special-for.content:
columns
options:
  variant: columns
  depth: 2
layout:
  position: footer
The first level as column headings, their children below. The grid fills the width with as many
columns as fit at a minimum width of --quartz-nav-column-min-width (default 10rem). The classic
footer sitemap.


                  
                   columns.max
                  
                

The option is meant to limit the number of columns but currently has no effect — the grid
follows the width alone. For fewer columns, increase the minimum width.


select
options:
  variant: select
  title: Jump to
  select:
    button: false   # default
A <select> jump menu. First-level folders become option groups, their folder page appears in
them as “Overview”; deeper levels are indented. As long as the current page is not in the list, the
menu shows “Jump to…”.
How it navigates: chosen with the mouse, it goes right away. Chosen with the keyboard, it waits
for Enter — otherwise the page would jump while you arrow through the options. select.button: true
adds a “Go” button next to it, for sites that want an explicit step.
The menu navigates through Quartz’s own page transitions and needs JavaScript. Here title
becomes the menu’s label.
Often a select is not the navigation itself but its mobile version: mobile: select puts the same
menu in place of a list below the mobile breakpoint (6.1).
pager
options:
  variant: pager
layout:
  position: afterBody
“Previous” and “Next”, each with the title of the neighbouring page and an arrow. There is one below
every text on this website.
In what order
options:
  pager:
    order: tree   # tree (default) | siblings

















pager.orderPages through …treethe whole scope in reading order: folder page, then its children, then the next foldersiblingsonly the neighbours in the same folder; the end of the folder is the end
With tree the scope decides how far it goes (chapter 3):

scope: root pages through the whole site — or through rootPath.
scope: section stops at the end of the section.
depth limits the depth.

Folders without a link target are skipped, as is a folder that leads to the same page as its first
entry (3.3). On the first page “Previous” is missing, on the
last “Next”; if a page has neither, nothing appears.
Labels
options:
  pager:
    labels: false   # arrow and title only
The words “Previous” and “Next” follow the page’s language on a multilingual site, otherwise the
site’s language (7.3).

en/navigations/4-variants/index.title: 4 – The ten variants
en/navigations/4-variants/index.content:
variant chooses the form. Every variant brings its own direction — vertical or horizontal —, there
is no separate option for it.







































































VariantDirectionIn shortBelongs intreeverticaleverything visible, nestedsidebaraccordionverticalfolders expandsidebarflyoutverticalfolders open a panel beside themsidebarbarhorizontalone row, sublevels behindheader, footerdropdownhorizontalrow, folders open a menu belowheadermegahorizontalrow, menu with columnsheadertabshorizontaltabs, children of the active one belowheader, above the textcolumnsgridcolumn headings with entriesfooterselect—jump menuwherever space is shortpager—“Previous” / “Next”below the text





















PageContent4.1 – Verticaltree, accordion, flyout4.2 – Horizontalbar, dropdown, mega, tabs and align4.3 – Special formscolumns, select, pager


                  
                  The form is not the scope 
                  
                

Which part of the tree goes into the form is decided by rootPath, scope and depth
(chapter 3). Every variant can be combined with every scope.

en/navigations/5-interaction/01-folder-r.title: 5.1 – Folder rows
en/navigations/5-interaction/01-folder-r.content:
folderClick — expand or link
The whole row of an expandable folder is the click target. What it does is decided by
folderClick:
options:
  folderClick: toggle   # toggle (default) | link
toggle — a click anywhere on the row opens or closes the folder. The folder page can then only be
reached from this navigation through an extra entry: indexEntry: first puts “Overview” into the
folder as its first child (3.2).
link — the row is a link to the folder page, and a separate expand button with the chevron sits
at its right edge. That is the usual choice together with trigger: hover: the menu opens on hover,
the click follows the link (5.2).






























togglelinkClick on the titleexpandsopens the folder pageChevrona hint, not a button of its owna button of its own, always visibleFolder page reachable viaindexEntry: firstthe titleFor screen readersone control with the titlea link and a button “Expand …”


                  
                  Folders that only expand on mobile 
                  
                

With mobile: accordion, folders in tree, bar, tabs and columns expand only on smartphones
(6.1). They always use link and button, whatever folderClick
says — on the desktop their title should stay a link.


chevrons — the arrow
options:
  chevrons: false
Hides the chevron on folders with folderClick: toggle. With link it stays, because there it is the
button. Which symbol the chevron is, is set by iconNames.chevron (7.1).
Open or closed




















OptionDefaultEffectfolderDefaultStatecollapsedopen makes all folders start openexpandActivetruefolders on the path to the current page start open
Both apply to accordion. The menus of dropdown and mega and the panels of flyout always
start closed — a menu that is already open on load covers the page.
exclusive — one folder per level
options:
  variant: accordion
  exclusive: true
Opening a folder closes the open one next to it. The browser does this itself through the name
attribute of <details> — without a script, in current browsers. Older ones leave several open.
persistState — memory
options:
  variant: accordion
  persistState: true
  id: sidebar
Which folders someone opened or closed is remembered by the browser in localStorage and restored on
the next page. The path to the current page still stays open as long as expandActive applies —
a remembered “closed” does not win against the page you are on.


                  
                  With persistState, always an id
                  
                

It is stored under the navigation’s ID. Without id that is a checksum of all options — change any
of them later and the memory is gone. A fixed id keeps it across changes
(7.3).


Menus and panels (dropdown, mega, flyout) are never remembered.

en/navigations/5-interaction/02-click-or.title: 5.2 – Click or hover
en/navigations/5-interaction/02-click-or.content:
trigger
options:
  variant: dropdown
  trigger: hover   # click (default) | hover
  folderClick: link
Applies to dropdown, mega and flyout.
click opens a menu when its folder is clicked. That works everywhere, even without a script.
hover opens it on hover and — so keyboard users are not left out — also as soon as an entry
inside receives focus. On leaving it closes after a short delay, so a menu does not snap shut when the
mouse cuts a corner.
Hover only exists on devices that support it. On a smartphone or tablet click applies automatically.


                  
                   hover belongs with folderClick: link
                  
                

With toggle, a click closes the menu that hovering had already opened. With link, hovering opens
the menu and the click leads to the folder page — which is what you expect from a menu bar.


How menus close

Opening another one closes the open one on the same level.
A click elsewhere closes all menus of this navigation.
Escape closes all and puts focus back on the folder whose menu it came from.
A page change closes all before the new page appears.

Where a panel moves to
When a panel opens, the script checks whether it has room.
flyout in the right half. With flyout.side: auto the panels open to the left when the
navigation sits in the right half of the window — otherwise they would stick out. The chevron then
points left. right and left switch the check off.
dropdown and mega at the right edge. A menu that would stick out of the window on the right
hangs from the right edge of its entry instead of the left.
In a column that clips. If the sidebar scrolls on its own, or fades out softly at the bottom, it
would cut a panel off. The panel is then lifted out of the column — into the browser’s top layer, in
older browsers with a fixed position — and anchored to its row. Because a position anchored like that
does not move along when scrolling, it closes as soon as you scroll.

en/navigations/5-interaction/03-without-.title: 5.3 – Without JavaScript
en/navigations/5-interaction/03-without-.content:
The navigation is finished HTML when it arrives in the browser. The script adds things but changes
nothing the structure relies on.
What works without the script

































WhatWith whatAll links, active page, active pathwritten at build timeExpanding and collapsing folders<details> and <summary>Menus of dropdown, mega, flyout by clickalso <details>One folder per level (exclusive)the name attribute of <details>Opening and closing the mobile menu behind the burger buttona checkbox and CSSSwitching at the mobile breakpointmedia queries
What the script adds













































WhatWithout the scriptpersistStatenothing is rememberedtrigger: hovermenus only open by clickClosing menus on a click elsewhere, Escape, page changethey stay open until their folder is clicked againMoving panels and lifting them out of columnspanels can stick out of the window or be cut offHolding the page still behind the mobile menu, Escapethe page scrolls alongNavigating with select and mobile: selectthe menu does nothingClosing folders that only expand on mobile on smartphonesthey stay openOpen animationfolders open without transitionScrolling the active page into view in a long sidebarit stays where it is
Why the animation needs the script
Folders that are already open on load — the active path, a remembered state — should not slide open on
every page change. The animation is therefore tied to an attribute that the script only sets when
someone touches the folder for the first time. Without the script there is no attribute, and without
the attribute no animation.
Anyone who has reduced motion in their operating system (prefers-reduced-motion) gets none anyway.
